title: 8  What probability means, and the robot
section: 8.5 The robot as a universal reasoner, and its limits
text:
8.5 The robot as a universal reasoner, and its limits
The robot handles its information consistently, and Cox’s theorem says it does so in the only way that is consistent. It is natural to push the construction to its limit and ask what it would become. Give the robot a prior over every hypothesis it could state, the rules of Chapter 6 to update that prior, and unlimited time to compute. Do we then obtain a perfect thinking machine — a universal reasoner, in the sense in which a Turing machine or von Neumann’s stored-program computer is a universal calculator, able to reach any thought that inference can reach?
The limit is a definite mathematical object. A prior over all computable hypotheses, each weighted by \(2^{-K(h)}\) — where \(K(h)\), the Kolmogorov complexity of \(h\), is the length of the shortest program that generates it — is Solomonoff’s universal prior; conditionalising it on data is Solomonoff induction, and its decision-theoretic extension to an agent that also acts is AIXI (Hutter).38 The weighting is Occam’s razor written as a probability distribution: a simpler hypothesis, having a shorter description, receives more prior mass. The optimality is not merely asserted — this predictor provably dominates every computable predictor and converges on the truth, in a precise sense, faster than any of them. So the intuition that an optimal updating rule fed rich enough information yields the best possible inference is not naive; it is a theorem about a specific object. The universal thinker exists, as mathematics.
The same theory that defines it also states three things that dismantle “perfect thinking machine”, and they fail at different depths. A fourth objection arrives from a different direction — from logic rather than from computability — and bears on the robot in its everyday working form, not only on its idealised limit.
1. Coherence-optimal is not truth-optimal. Cox guarantees that the robot’s handling of information is consistent — that it cannot be Dutch-booked, that it extends Boolean logic uniquely. It guarantees nothing about convergence to the truth. A perfectly coherent Bayesian working with a misspecified model updates optimally, confidently, and coherently towards the wrong answer: when the truth lies outside the hypothesis space, the posterior concentrates not on the truth but on the pseudo-true value — the member of the model class closest to reality in Kullback–Leibler divergence, the information-theoretic measure of how far one distribution is from another.39 “Handles its information in the best possible way” is true, but silently indexed to the model class the robot was given. The optimality is conditional, and the condition is supplied from outside the calculus.
2. Convergence presupposes that the truth is already in the space. The results that vindicate “rich data washes out the prior” — posterior consistency, the Bernstein–von Mises theorem, and the merging of opinions cited earlier in the point-null discussion — each require the true data-generating process to lie in the support of the prior (for merging, that the two priors be mutually absolutely continuous).40 Cromwell’s rule, met in the hypothesis-space section of this chapter, states the barrier in one line: a hypothesis assigned prior probability zero keeps posterior probability zero whatever the evidence. So “if the information is rich enough” already presupposes the hard part. Conditionalisation is a horizontal operation: it redistributes probability within a fixed set of possibilities. It contains no rule for the vertical move of enlarging that set — of inventing “germ”, “natural selection”, or “the curvature of spacetime”, concepts that were not points in the prior space at all. This is the problem of new hypotheses in confirmation theory, met at small scale in the alternating-coin example: neither Bayes’ rule nor Cox’s desiderata contain a procedure for extending their own space of possibilities.41 Run forever on rich data, the ideal machine finds only the best hypothesis it could already state.
3. The universal-computer analogy imports the wrong universality — and the right one cannot be built. Turing and von Neumann universality concerns what is computable given a program, in principle, ignoring resources. Two things must be dropped to get from there to a universal thinker. The program is exogenous — it is the analogue of the prior, so universality relocates the question of which thought to think rather than answering it — and universality says nothing about tractability. Here the conclusion is decisive: Solomonoff induction is uncomputable, because Kolmogorov complexity is uncomputable (evaluating it reduces to the halting problem); AIXI is uncomputable; and exact Bayesian inference over a rich hypothesis space is intractable even where it is computable, the evidence integral being #P-hard or worse.42 The moment “perfect universal Bayesian thinker” is made precise, the proof of its optimality arrives bundled with a proof that no physical machine can be it. The gap between a real reasoner and the ideal is therefore not an engineering shortfall to be closed; it is a theorem. Every actual thinker is a resource-bounded approximation to an uncomputable ideal.
4. The calculus grades propositions; it cannot express relations among objects. The first three limits concern what the robot can compute and what its prior can reach. This one concerns what its language can say, and it is visible in the derivation rather than in the ideal. Both routes to the calculus take a Boolean algebra of propositions as given and define probability as a function on it: the calculus supplies the grading, and the algebra supplies everything else. A Boolean algebra is precisely the algebraic content of the propositional logic of Chapter 3, so the robot inherits that logic’s expressive ceiling along with its rules. Propositional logic cannot reason from a generalisation to an instance — which is why the Socrates syllogism had to be handled one level down in Chapter 3 — and neither, by itself, can probability theory.
Notation hides the gap. Write \(P(\text{disease} \mid \text{exposure}) = 0.4\) and the intended reading is a generalisation: any person who is exposed has probability 0.4 of being diseased. The formalism contains no “any”. To probability theory, “exposure” is an opaque label for an event that either obtains or does not; it cannot look inside the label to see that a person is being quantified over, still less that two or three distinct individuals stand in a relation. Predicate logic supplies what is missing, with quantifiers and bound variables — \(\forall x: P(\text{disease}(x) \mid \text{exposure}(x)) = 0.4\) — where the binding of \(x\) does work the vertical bar cannot do. Most of that expression is logic; only the \(P\) is probability.43 Statistical practice has always known this without saying it, because the missing quantifier is written down somewhere else: the for (i in 1:N) loop in a model file is a universal quantifier, the plate in a graphical model is that quantifier drawn as a box, and the subscript in \(y_i \sim \text{Normal}(\mu_i, \sigma)\) binds a variable over units. None of this is in the sum and product rules, and none of it is derivable from them. Formalising the combination is a research field in its own right, in which measures over the sentences of a first-order language have been constructed and relational probabilistic languages are in practical use; what the field lacks is not a system but a canonical one with tolerable complexity.44
Two consequences matter for this book. The first is a warning about diagnosis: when a probabilistic analysis goes wrong, the error is often not in the probability. The arithmetic is right and the software ran, and what failed was the logical bookkeeping — which unit, which time point, which contrast, quantified how — carried out informally because the calculus offered nowhere to write it down. The second is that the structure Part III adds is precisely the structure the calculus lacks. A causal diagram is not a function of the joint distribution: distinct graphs can imply the same joint distribution and different consequences under intervention, so the graph carries information the probabilities do not contain (Chapter 12). Potential-outcome notation is predicate notation, \(Y_i(a)\) taking a unit and a treatment value as its arguments, and its central assumption is an explicitly quantified sentence — for every unit \(i\), if \(A_i = a\) then \(Y_i = Y_i(a)\) (Chapter 11). On this reading Part III is not an application of the robot’s calculus but a supplement to it, supplying in a second formalism the relational structure that graded belief cannot state. The robot is the right account of how evidence should move belief; it was never an account of how to say what the belief is about.
Two further limits are more specific but equally real. The first is logical omniscience. Classical Bayesianism assumes the agent already assigns probability 1 to every logical truth — that it knows all consequences of its own beliefs and has proved every theorem its axioms imply. No bounded reasoner is like this: we do not know whether Goldbach’s conjecture follows from the axioms of arithmetic, and a machine reasoning about unproved mathematics must be genuinely uncertain about claims that are either necessarily true or necessarily false. This logical uncertainty is a gap in the Cox–Jaynes ideal, which leaves no room for being unsure whether a conjecture is a theorem; recent work tries to supply the missing piece.45 The second limit returns to causation. Even unlimited passive observation leaves causal structure underdetermined: a passive updater conditionalising on given data cannot climb from association to intervention (Part III), so “rich enough information” must mean the right kind of information — data from interventions — which a pure observer does not generate for itself. This is why the universal agent AIXI must act and experiment, not merely predict; and it raises a question probability theory does not answer, of which, among the infinitely many true propositions a machine could compute, are worth computing. Bayes says how to update a degree of belief; it does not say which question deserves the effort.
Modern AI systems sharpen these limits rather than escape them. A large pretrained model is arguably richer than the bare robot, because pretraining installs an enormous implicit hypothesis space, and in-context learning behaves like Bayesian model-averaging over it.46 But the space is fixed at pretraining: the model cannot place posterior weight on a concept absent from what it learned, and it remains a resource-bounded approximation to the uncomputable ideal. The wall has moved outward; it has not disappeared. The forecasting networks met earlier in this chapter make the same point from the other side — a trained model’s \(P(\text{rain})\) is the forecaster’s distribution, learned from past data, not a property of tomorrow’s atmosphere.
The cleanest statement of the whole result is this. The robot is the ideal engine for moving through a space of hypotheses; it is not the faculty that makes the space. Probability theory governs updating within a stated set of possibilities — which is why this book treats the prior and the hypothesis space as declared components of a model, open to criticism and revision like any other component. (The point-null example earlier in this chapter is the same fact in miniature: two analysts whose hypothesis spaces differ over a single value need never converge, however much data arrives.) The strongest objection to the distinction is that a sufficiently rich universal prior — Solomonoff’s, over all computable hypotheses — already contains every conceivable hypothesis as a point of non-zero mass, so that discovery collapses into ordinary updating within an already-universal space. The objection is correct about the mathematics, and that is precisely why it matters that the object which makes it correct is the uncomputable one: the completeness that would dissolve the problem of discovery is available only in the machine that provably cannot be built.

title: 8  What probability means, and the robot
text:
8.6 Challenges to the Bayesian position
The position this chapter has taken — probability is epistemic, the prior is a declared component of the model open to criticism, and counting and frequency are the special cases that arise when information is symmetric or data are plentiful — has been attacked from several directions, and stating it fairly means setting the attacks out. Appendix H does so at length; in brief, there are four.

A single-event probability “says nothing.” As a claim about meaning this imports the frequency definition and then notes that a single case has no frequency, which assumes the conclusion. The real point concerns evaluation: one forecast cannot be checked against one outcome, and a forecaster’s probabilities are validated over a whole record by their calibration (Chapter 2).
Radical uncertainty. Knight, Keynes and their successors hold that for many real questions no prior can be set at all. Savage’s representation theorem answers that a coherent agent’s preferences already contain a prior — but Ellsberg’s urn exhibits stable, widely shared preferences for known odds that no single prior represents, a violation of the sure-thing principle that survives reflection.
Sets of priors. The response that keeps the calculus carries a set of priors rather than one — imprecise probability, or robust Bayes — and reports lower and upper probabilities, with a decision rule such as maxmin expected utility. Its price is dilation: with a set of priors, conditioning on an observation can widen an interval rather than narrow it, and one cannot claim both deep ignorance and immunity from dilation.
Is ambiguity aversion irrational? It resists the reflection that dissolves the biases of Chapter 2, and it has normative axiomatisations of its own, so it is better read as a rival standard than as a mistake.

None of these refutes the calculus; each bounds the scope of one way of using it. For the work in this book — finite data, models with declared structure, priors that must survive criticism and sensitivity analysis — a single prior, varied and checked, is adequate, and the apparatus of sets of priors is held in reserve for the cases, flagged where they arise, in which a single prior would assert more than is known. The aim is unchanged from the chapter’s first page: to quantify the uncertainty that can be quantified, and to mark plainly the uncertainty that cannot.

title: 8  What probability means, and the robot
text:
8.7 Where this leads
The calculus is now grounded twice, and its numbers have a meaning: degrees of belief, constrained to be coherent, conditioned on stated information. The next chapter, Chapter 9, builds the one theorem this chapter kept in reserve, Bayes’ theorem, into the working engine of inference — the likelihood ratio as the weight of evidence, and the odds form in which the hypothesis space of this chapter is redistributed by data. After it, Chapter 10 puts the engine to work on data, with the prior as the declared component this chapter argued it should be. The challenges to the position are collected in Appendix H, and the frequentist alternative this chapter set aside is laid out, as the foil it remains, in Appendix G.

8  What probability means, and the robot

title: 8  What probability means, and the robot
text:
8.8 Key points

The calculus is forced twice over, by two independent routes. Chapter 6 reached the sum and product rules by counting; this chapter reaches the same rules from the robot’s desiderata (Cox) and from the requirement of no sure loss on graded commitments (the Dutch book). That counting and consistency deliver one calculus is the main reason to take it seriously as the logic of science.
The chapter’s first half concerns what the number means: probability is read as epistemic (a degree of belief) rather than aleatoric (a physical property of a repeatable set-up), because the epistemic reading keeps working for single cases and unique hypotheses where the frequency reading falls silent.
Probability attaches to propositions, so it is always the two-place \(P(A \mid I)\); reading the number as a property of the world is the mind-projection fallacy. The sample space is fixed by the experiment; the hypothesis space \(\mathcal{H}\) — the set of explanations the analyst entertains, each a probability law over \(\Omega\) rather than an event in it — is fixed by the analyst, and every posterior is a relative plausibility within the current \(\mathcal{H}\), never an absolute verdict. Conditioning redistributes mass within \(\mathcal{H}\) and can kill a hypothesis (zero likelihood), but only revision of \(\mathcal{H}\) can create one; embedding \(\mathcal{H}\) in a grand sample space of (hypothesis, outcome) pairs makes Bayes literal pebble-conditioning but freezes with the list it was built from. Model criticism is how the hypothesis space learns.
The whole calculus is two rules: the sum rule \(P(A) + P(\lnot A) = 1\) and the product rule \(P(A \land B) = P(A)\,P(B \mid A)\).
The called-off bet is the operational meaning of conditional probability: a commitment about B activated only when A turns out true — the three-valued structure of Chapter 3’s historical aside, put to work.
The calculus keeps Chapter 3’s promises: at probabilities 0 and 1 it reproduces the strong syllogisms, and it licenses the weak ones quantitatively — if A entails B, then \(P(A \mid B) = P(A)/P(B) \geq P(A)\).
Counting is the symmetric special case of the belief calculus: when information does not distinguish a finite set of cases, desideratum 3.3 makes them equally probable, and probability reduces to favourable-over-possible.
The fine print of the agreement: Cox’s theorem needs technical assumptions, and the belief road forces only finite — not countable — additivity. The roads also differ on what carries probability (propositions and single cases vs repeatable setups). None of this affects the working rules used in this book.
Within the epistemic reading, the subjective school (Ramsey, de Finetti, Savage) requires only coherence and expects agreement to emerge from shared data, while the objective school (Jeffreys, Jaynes) requires that the same information yield the same probability, and supplies symmetry, invariance, and maximum-entropy rules for the assignment. The dispute concerns where prior probabilities come from; both schools deny that probability is physical.
Pushed to its ideal limit — a prior over all computable hypotheses, updated without resource limit — the robot becomes Solomonoff induction (and, for an agent that also acts, AIXI): a provably optimal predictor that is nonetheless (i) only coherence-optimal, not truth-optimal — a misspecified model converges confidently to the pseudo-true value; (ii) able to update within a hypothesis space but never to enlarge it (the problem of new hypotheses); and (iii) uncomputable, so every real system — a large pretrained model included — is a resource-bounded approximation. The robot moves through a space of hypotheses; it does not make the space.
A fourth limit is about expression rather than computation. Probability grades propositions, and inherits the expressive ceiling of the propositional logic it extends: it cannot state a relation among several objects. A conditional probability contains no “for all”, so the quantifier is supplied informally by the reader, or written down elsewhere — in a for loop, a plate, a subscript over units. The structure Part III adds — causal graphs, and potential outcomes indexed by unit — is precisely the relational structure that graded belief cannot express.
Uncertainty has many sources — biological variation, sampling, the fitting algorithm, the model’s structure, the data’s structure, and the gap between what is modelled and what is wanted — and together they make predictions of complex phenomena over-confident, experts’ included. The scientist’s task is to turn unknown unknowns into quantified known unknowns, not to manufacture certainty.
The desiderata force the relations, not the values. The sum and product rules follow from consistency (desideratum 3.1) with 1 and 2; desideratum 3.3 read narrowly is uncontroversial, read as agreement across agents it is the objectivist thesis, and adopting the robot commits a reader to the calculus, not to objectivism.
Symmetric information fixes a prior only relative to a parametrisation. Indifference is a theorem about invariant information, extended by transformation groups and maximum entropy, but the cube factory and Bertrand’s chord show that “no information” yields different priors in different coordinates; uniqueness returns only when a group is supplied that the bare problem does not state.
The Bayesian position faces genuine challenges as well as misunderstandings (set out in full in Appendix H). A single-event probability is meaningful but is validated only over many forecasts, through calibration. Under radical uncertainty a sharp prior may not be elicitable, and Ellsberg’s experiment exhibits reproducible ambiguity aversion that violates Savage’s sure-thing principle, so no single prior represents the preferences. The disciplined response carries a set of priors (imprecise probability, robust Bayes) with a decision rule such as maxmin expected utility — at the cost of dilation, in which conditioning can widen rather than narrow the interval. These bound the scope of the single-prior workflow without refuting the calculus.

title: 8  What probability means, and the robot
text:
8.9 Exercises

Make your own Dutch book. A colleague prices a ticket on A at 0.60 and a ticket on NOT A at 0.55. Construct the trades that guarantee the colleague a loss, and compute the loss. Then do the same for prices 0.30 and 0.50 (note the direction of trade reverses).
The second weak syllogism. Suppose A entails B (\(P(B \mid A) = 1\)), with \(0 < P(A) < 1\) and \(P(B) < 1\). Using the decomposition \(P(B) = P(B \mid A)P(A) + P(B \mid \lnot A)P(\lnot A)\), show that \(P(B \mid \lnot A) \leq P(B)\): learning that A is false makes B less plausible. State the condition under which the inequality is strict.
Extend the mini-sim. For the clinic example, compute the probability that at least one of the two selected patients is a carrier, three ways: by counting (complement of choosing both from the 7 non-carriers), by the sum and product rules, and by extending the Monte Carlo chunk. Confirm the three answers agree.
Conditional probabilities in the cohort. Source R/simulate_cohort.R and generate the master cohort. By counting rows, estimate \(P(\text{stroke} \mid \text{drug})\) and \(P(\text{stroke} \mid \lnot\text{drug})\), and verify the product rule numerically: \(P(\text{stroke} \land \text{drug}) = P(\text{drug}) \cdot P(\text{stroke} \mid \text{drug})\). These conditional probabilities are associational quantities; why they must not be read as the effect of the drug is the subject of Chapter 4 and Chapter 11.
The single case. The forecast says there is a 70% chance of rain tomorrow. Explain what this number means on the belief road and what auxiliary construction the counting road needs to make sense of it. Which parts of the construction are testable?
The called-off bet, reversed. An agent prices \(P(A) = 0.5\), \(P(A \land B) = 0.2\), but the conditional ticket on “B given A” at \(q = 0.3\) (the coherent price is 0.4). Adapt the Dutch book chunk to construct the sure loss against this agent, and verify that the loss per unit equals \(P(A \land B) - q \cdot P(A)\).
The limits of the universal thinker. A colleague argues: “Give a Bayesian machine a prior over every computable hypothesis and unlimited compute, and it will eventually think every thought worth thinking.” Using the limits set out in this chapter, write a short reply. (a) In what sense is such a machine provably optimal, and in what sense is that optimality merely conditional? (b) Explain why conditioning on more data cannot, by itself, give non-zero probability to a hypothesis the prior excluded, and name one historical concept whose introduction would have required exactly that move. (c) State the result that makes the ideal machine physically unrealisable, and say what it implies about the relation between real AI systems and the ideal. (d) A second colleague replies that the machine’s language is adequate because “we can always say the rest in English”. Take a conditional probability of your choice, state the generalisation it is meant to express, and identify what the English is doing that the calculus is not — then name the piece of ordinary statistical notation in which that work is normally written down.

A survey of the frequency and propensity theories and their difficulties is Gillies D, Philosophical Theories of Probability, London: Routledge, 2000.↩︎

The difficulty, now called Humphreys’s paradox, is that the multiplication axiom and Bayes’ theorem require the inverse conditional \(P(\text{condition} \mid \text{outcome})\) to exist and behave as a probability, whereas a propensity is a time-directed causal disposition for which that inverse has no interpretation; subsequent work has explored weakening either the axioms or the propensity reading rather than abandoning one.↩︎
Comte A, Cours de philosophie positive, Paris: Bachelier, 1830-1842; von Mises R, Positivism: A Study in Human Understanding, Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1951 (German original Kleines Lehrbuch des Positivismus, The Hague: Van Stockum, 1939). Reichenbach co-founded the Berlin Society for Empirical Philosophy, the logical-empiricist group allied with the Vienna Circle.↩︎
Fisher RA, Statistical Methods for Research Workers, Edinburgh: Oliver & Boyd, 1925; Neyman J, Pearson ES, “On the Problem of the Most Efficient Tests of Statistical Hypotheses,” Philos Trans R Soc Lond A 1933;231:289-337 (DOI); Neyman J, “Outline of a Theory of Statistical Estimation Based on the Classical Theory of Probability,” Philos Trans R Soc Lond A 1937;236:333-380 (DOI) — the origin of the confidence interval.↩︎
Of course, we could ask for the probability that the coin is fair, but we already know this probability to be zero, as no coin is completely fair.↩︎
Jaynes ET, Probability Theory: The Logic of Science (Bretthorst GL, ed.), Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 2003. The fallacy — attributing to the world what belongs to the reasoner’s state of knowledge — is a recurring theme of the book.↩︎
Jaynes ET, Probability Theory: The Logic of Science (Bretthorst GL, ed.), Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 2003 (ch. 4, on multiple hypothesis testing, where surprising data revive hypotheses that were given negligible standing at the outset).↩︎
The name is Lindley’s, after Cromwell’s 1650 plea to the Church of Scotland (“think it possible you may be mistaken”): Lindley DV, Making Decisions, 2nd ed., London: Wiley, 1985.↩︎
Savage LJ, The Foundations of Statistics, New York: Wiley, 1954 (2nd revised ed. New York: Dover, 1972). Ramsey’s and de Finetti’s foundational papers are cited in the Dutch book section below.↩︎
Blackwell D, Dubins L, “Merging of Opinions with Increasing Information,” Ann Math Statist 1962;33:882-886 (DOI). The result requires the two priors to be mutually absolutely continuous; where they are mutually singular on an event — as a continuous and a spike-and-slab prior are on \(\{\theta = 0\}\) — it does not apply there.↩︎
Lindley DV, “A Statistical Paradox,” Biometrika 1957;44:187-192 (DOI); Bartlett MS, “A comment on D. V. Lindley’s statistical paradox,” Biometrika 1957;44:533-534 (DOI). The Bayesian point-null test, and the dependence of its verdict on the slab, originate with Jeffreys H, Theory of Probability, 3rd ed., Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1961.↩︎
Jaynes ET, “Information Theory and Statistical Mechanics,” Phys Rev 1957;106:620-630 (DOI); Jaynes ET, “Prior Probabilities,” IEEE Trans Syst Sci Cybern 1968;4:227-241 (DOI).↩︎
Long-run betting performance measures neither; it tracks calibration, an external standard. It happens to correlate with the objectivist’s extra clause, which is why a wager seems to favour the better-calibrated agent — but the subjectivist bites the bullet that a rational agent can be coherent, well-reasoned by its own lights, and still lose.↩︎
The non-uniqueness is structural, not merely practical. Parametrisation. The principle of indifference is not invariant under a change of variable: a density that is flat in a parameter is not flat in its square or its logarithm, so the instruction to give indistinguishable cases equal probability returns different answers according to how the cases are described. The classical demonstration is Bertrand’s chord problem, in which three equally natural descriptions of a “random” chord yield three different probabilities (Bertrand J, Calcul des probabilités, Paris: Gauthier-Villars, 1889); Jaynes’s transformation-group rule resolves such a problem only where the stated information carries a definite symmetry. Constraints and reference measure. Maximum entropy removes the ambiguity only after the analyst has fixed which constraints to impose and, on a continuous space, a reference measure against which entropy is defined; different admissible choices give different priors, and neither is determined by the information. The Jeffreys prior is invariant under reparametrisation — that is its purpose — but is computed from the Fisher information, a feature of the sampling model, so it depends on which experiment produced the data rather than on the parameter alone. Coherence. The priors these rules produce are frequently improper, and impropriety can generate the marginalisation paradox, in which two valid derivations of the same posterior quantity disagree (Dawid AP, Stone M, Zidek JV, “Marginalization Paradoxes in Bayesian and Structural Inference,” J R Stat Soc Series B 1973;35:189-233 (DOI)). The attempt to fix a prior by rule can therefore conflict with the coherence requirement both schools accept. None of this makes objective priors useless: where the information carries a genuine symmetry they are well defined and command wide agreement. It shows only that “the information fixes the prior” holds in special cases, not as a general rule.↩︎
Reference priors derive a default by maximising the information the data are expected to supply about the parameter, so that the prior’s own contribution is minimal (Bernardo JM, “Reference Posterior Distributions for Bayesian Inference,” J R Stat Soc Series B 1979;41:113-147 (DOI)). Weakly informative priors instead impose deliberately mild bounds that exclude implausible values and regularise the estimate without encoding specific subject-matter knowledge (Gelman A, Jakulin A, Pittau MG, Su YS, “A Weakly Informative Default Prior Distribution for Logistic and Other Regression Models,” Ann Appl Stat 2008;2:1360-1383 (DOI)). For the argument that the subjective/objective division is itself too coarse to classify these practices, see Gelman A, Hennig C, “Beyond Subjective and Objective in Statistics,” J R Stat Soc Series A 2017;180:967-1033 (DOI).↩︎
Two examples show what “deriving” a prior means. Invariance. Suppose the parameter \(\sigma\) is a scale — a standard deviation, say — and the stated information does not include the units of measurement. A prior that carries no information about scale must then have the same form whether \(\sigma\) is recorded in days or in hours, i.e. its shape must not change when \(\sigma\) is multiplied by a positive constant. The only density with this property is \(p(\sigma) \propto 1/\sigma\), which is a flat prior on \(\log \sigma\). Jeffreys generalised this style of argument into a rule — the Jeffreys prior, proportional to the square root of the Fisher information — which returns the same posterior whichever smooth transformation of the parameter the analyst works with (Jeffreys H, “An invariant form for the prior probability in estimation problems,” Proc R Soc Lond A Math Phys Sci 1946;186:453-461 (DOI)). Maximum entropy. The entropy of a distribution is a single number measuring how spread out the distribution is — equivalently, how little it commits to beyond what is stated. The rule is: express the available information as constraints, then adopt the distribution with the largest entropy among all distributions satisfying those constraints; any other choice encodes information that was not stated. Three standard results. With no constraints beyond a finite list of possible outcomes, the maximum-entropy distribution is the uniform — the symmetry argument recovered as a special case. For a positive quantity with a stated mean, it is the exponential distribution. For a quantity on the real line with stated mean and variance, it is the normal distribution. (These distributions are introduced in Chapter 7.)↩︎
O’Hagan A, “Expert Knowledge Elicitation: Subjective but Scientific,” Am Stat 2019;73:69-81 (DOI); a book-length treatment of the methodology is O’Hagan A, Buck CE, Daneshkhah A, Eiser JR, Garthwaite PH, Jenkinson DJ, Oakley JE, Rakow T, Uncertain Judgements: Eliciting Experts’ Probabilities, Chichester: Wiley, 2006.↩︎
Genest C, Zidek JV, “Combining Probability Distributions: A Critique and an Annotated Bibliography,” Statist Sci 1986;1:114-135 (DOI).↩︎
Quantum mechanics describes a physical system by a mathematical object called the quantum state (in the simplest case a wave function, \(\psi\)). The state evolves deterministically in time, according to the Schrödinger equation; probability enters the theory at a single point, when a measurement is made. The Born rule states that the quantum state attaches to each possible measurement outcome a complex number, the amplitude, and that the probability of an outcome is the squared magnitude of its amplitude. The rule is a separate postulate — it does not follow from the rest of the formalism — and it is the source of every probability that quantum theory predicts; those predictions are among the most precisely confirmed in physics. The interpretations of quantum mechanics differ on what the rule’s probabilities are: a physical propensity of the system, a relative frequency across branching worlds, or — the QBist reading — a normative constraint on the beliefs of the agent who measures. Jaynes ET, Probability Theory: The Logic of Science (Bretthorst GL, ed.), Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 2003 (chapters 1–2).↩︎

Aristotelian term logic is a logic of quantified categories (“all men are mortal”), and is stronger than the propositional logic of Chapter 3; “Aristotelian” in Jaynes’s usage means only bivalent — every proposition is either true or false — and is his contrast with the many-valued logics of the historical aside in Chapter 3. What the robot requires is bivalence, so that is the word used here. The difference between the two senses matters again in the fourth limit below.↩︎
Cox RT, “Probability, frequency and reasonable expectation,” Am J Phys 1946;14:1-13 (DOI).↩︎
Ramsey FP, “Truth and Probability” (written 1926), in Braithwaite RB (ed.), The Foundations of Mathematics and other Logical Essays, London: Kegan Paul, Trench, Trubner & Co., 1931:156-198; de Finetti B, “La prévision: ses lois logiques, ses sources subjectives,” Ann Inst Henri Poincaré 1937;7:1-68 (text).↩︎
Reference priors derive a default by maximising the information the data are expected to supply about the parameter, so that the prior’s own contribution is minimal (Bernardo JM, “Reference Posterior Distributions for Bayesian Inference,” J R Stat Soc Series B 1979;41:113-147 (DOI)). Weakly informative priors instead impose deliberately mild bounds that exclude implausible values and regularise the estimate without encoding specific subject-matter knowledge (Gelman A, Jakulin A, Pittau MG, Su YS, “A Weakly Informative Default Prior Distribution for Logistic and Other Regression Models,” Ann Appl Stat 2008;2:1360-1383 (DOI)). For the argument that the subjective/objective division is itself too coarse to classify these practices, see Gelman A, Hennig C, “Beyond Subjective and Objective in Statistics,” J R Stat Soc Series A 2017;180:967-1033 (DOI).↩︎
van Fraassen BC, Laws and Symmetry, Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1989 (the cube factory).↩︎
The problem is due to Bertrand J, Calcul des probabilités, Paris: Gauthier-Villars, 1889; the invariance resolution is Jaynes ET, “The Well-Posed Problem,” Found Phys 1973;3:477-493 (DOI).↩︎
Van Horn KS, “Constructing a logic of plausible inference: a guide to Cox’s theorem,” Int J Approx Reason 2003;34:3-24.↩︎
Solomonoff RJ, “A formal theory of inductive inference. Part I,” Inf Control 1964;7:1-22; “Part II,” Inf Control 1964;7:224-254. The decision-theoretic extension, to an agent that acts as well as predicts, is AIXI: Hutter M, Universal Artificial Intelligence: Sequential Decisions Based on Algorithmic Probability, Berlin: Springer, 2005.↩︎
Berk RH, “Limiting behavior of posterior distributions when the model is incorrect,” Ann Math Statist 1966;37:51-58 (DOI). When the true distribution is not in the model class, the posterior concentrates on the member of the class minimising the Kullback–Leibler divergence to the truth — the pseudo-true value.↩︎
The classical consistency theorem is Doob JL, “Application of the theory of martingales,” in Le Calcul des Probabilités et ses Applications, Paris: CNRS, 1949:23-27; the Bernstein–von Mises theorem and the consistency theory are set out in van der Vaart AW, Asymptotic Statistics, Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1998 (ch. 10). Cromwell’s rule — that a prior of 0 or 1 is never revised by any evidence — is due to Lindley DV, Making Decisions, 2nd ed., London: Wiley, 1985. The merging-of-opinions result is Blackwell and Dubins, cited in the point-null discussion above.↩︎
That Bayesian conditionalisation redistributes probability among the hypotheses already entertained, and has no rule for enlarging its own space, is the problem of new hypotheses (or new theories): Glymour C, Theory and Evidence, Princeton: Princeton University Press, 1980; Earman J, Bayes or Bust? A Critical Examination of Bayesian Confirmation Theory, Cambridge, MA: MIT Press, 1992 (ch. 5).↩︎
Kolmogorov complexity is uncomputable — evaluating it reduces to the halting problem — so Solomonoff’s universal prior and AIXI are uncomputable; see Li M, Vitányi P, An Introduction to Kolmogorov Complexity and Its Applications, 4th ed., Cham: Springer, 2019. Even for a computable model class, exact probabilistic inference over a rich space is intractable: Roth D, “On the hardness of approximate reasoning,” Artif Intell 1996;82:273-302 (DOI), which shows the relevant counting problems are #P-hard.↩︎
Chapman D, “Probability theory does not extend logic,” Meta-rationality, 21 August 2015 (text). The essay develops the expressiveness point at length, and also charges Jaynes with conflating propositional, Aristotelian and predicate logic. The textual part of the charge holds: in the “Nitpicking” comments of chapter 1 of Probability Theory: The Logic of Science, Jaynes dismisses the quantifiers of predicate calculus as mere abbreviations for the English phrases “for all” and “there is a” — exactly the identification that Frege’s analysis of nested quantification refuted, since no abbreviation distinguishes “every boy loves some girl” from “some girl is loved by every boy”. Jaynes’s careful claim, that Aristotelian deductive logic is the limiting form of the rules for plausible reasoning, is correct; the preface’s claim that probability theory supplies the uniquely valid principles of logic in general is not, and the two sit a few pages apart. Chapman’s further account of how the error arose — a confusion with the 1930s vogue for “non-Aristotelian” many-valued logic — is offered without a source and is best read as reconstruction rather than history. It is also worth noticing that the two parties agree about the mechanics and differ about what they signify: Jaynes holds that plain English supplies all the quantification a physicist needs, and Chapman that plain English is then doing the logical work for which the calculus is being given credit.↩︎
Probability measures over the sentences of a first-order language were constructed by Gaifman H, “Concerning measures in first order calculi,” Israel J Math 1964;2:1-18 (DOI). The systematic analysis of the resulting logics — including the distinction between placing probability on the domain, which yields statistical generalisations, and on possible worlds, which yields degrees of belief — is Halpern JY, “An analysis of first-order logics of probability,” Artif Intell 1990;46:311-350 (DOI); the general systems are expressive but computationally forbidding, which is why none has become standard. Practical relational formalisms attach weights to first-order formulae instead of seeking a complete logic: Richardson M, Domingos P, “Markov logic networks,” Mach Learn 2006;62:107-136 (DOI). Carnap’s inductive logic was an earlier attempt at the same marriage, and is instructive about where the difficulty lies: it was developed for languages of monadic predicates and did not extend cleanly to relational ones (Carnap R, Logical Foundations of Probability, Chicago: University of Chicago Press, 1950).↩︎
The assumption at issue is logical omniscience; the attempt to model a reasoner uncertain about the consequences of its own axioms is Garrabrant S, Benson-Tilsen T, Critch A, Soares N, Taylor J, “Logical Induction,” arXiv:1609.03543, 2016. This is distinct from, and does not depend on, the Lucas–Penrose argument that Gödel’s theorems show human minds are not machines (Lucas JR, “Minds, Machines and Gödel,” Philosophy 1961;36:112-127; Penrose R, The Emperor’s New Mind, Oxford: Oxford University Press, 1989), which is widely regarded as an overreach.↩︎
Xie SM, Raghunathan A, Liang P, Ma T, “An Explanation of In-context Learning as Implicit Bayesian Inference,” International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR), 2022 (arXiv:2111.02080). The claim is that a model pretrained on data with long-range structure performs, at inference time, something close to Bayesian averaging over a latent concept — within the hypothesis space fixed at pretraining.↩︎

8  What probability means, and the robot

title: 9  Bayes’ theorem and the weight of evidence
text:
9.1 Prior, likelihood, and posterior
Prior probability \(P(\text{Hypothesis} \vert I)\) is a purely logical term that incorporates all relevant evidence that is not present in the data. The separation of evidence into “data” and “prior” is a matter of convenience of calculation, nothing more. Every probability in this chapter is conditional on the background information \(I\) of Chapter 8; following custom, \(I\) is written once here and then suppressed from the notation, but it never leaves the inference — the prior is where most of it enters.
Likelihood \(P(\text{data} \vert \text{Hypothesis})\) models how probable the sample data are under each member of the hypothesis space \(\mathcal{H}\) of Chapter 8 — the list of explanations the analyst is prepared to entertain, as distinct from the sample space of possible data. If \(\mathcal{H} = \{H_1, H_2\}\), then the likelihood has two members as well: \(P(\text{data} \vert H_1)\) is the probability of seeing the sample data if it happens that \(H_1\) is true, and \(P(\text{data} \vert H_2)\) is the probability of seeing the sample data if it happens that \(H_2\) is true. If the likelihood ratio \(LR = \frac{P(\text{data} \vert H_1)}{P(\text{data} \vert H_2)} = 1\), then the data are irrelevant. \(LR = 10\) means that the data support \(H_1\) ten times more than \(H_2\).
The fact that the sample data provide much more evidence for \(H_1\) than for \(H_2\) does not by itself mean that we should think \(H_1\) more probable than \(H_2\), or than any other logically possible hypothesis. Likelihoods do not sum to one over the hypothesis space. Therefore likelihood is not a probability.
Posterior probability \(P(\text{Hypothesis} \vert \text{data})\) is the product of prior and likelihood for each member of the hypothesis space, normalised so that the probabilities sum to one over the hypothesis space. The posterior distribution is the output of Bayesian inference: the probability distribution that holds our beliefs about the parameter values, after the data.

9  Bayes' theorem and the weight of evidence

title: 9  Bayes’ theorem and the weight of evidence
text:
9.2 Bayes’ theorem
We can derive Bayes’ theorem straight from the definition of conditional probability (Chapter 6),
\[P(A\vert B) = \frac{P(A \land B)}{P(B)},\]
and equivalently \[P(B\vert A) = \frac{P(B \land A)}{P(A)}.\]
As \(P(A \land B) = P(B \land A)\),
\[P(A\vert B)\,P(B) = P(B\vert A)\,P(A),\] and so
\[P(A\vert B) =\frac{P(A)\,P(B\vert A)}{P(B)}.\] This is Bayes’ theorem. Now let us substitute hypothesis \(H\) for \(A\) and data \(d\) for \(B\):
\[P(H \vert d) =\frac{P(H)\,P(d\vert H)}{P(d)}.\] Here \(P(H\vert d)\) is the posterior, \(P(H)\) is the prior probability of the hypothesis, \(P(d\vert H)\) is the likelihood (the probability of the data given the hypothesis), and \(P(d)\) is the total probability of the data, summed over all the hypotheses in the hypothesis space. \(P(d)\) is the normalising constant, which guarantees that the posterior probabilities sum to one over the hypothesis space.
The single most important thing to remember is that the posterior is proportional to the product of prior and likelihood.
What does \(P(d)\) really mean? If \(\mathcal{H} = \{H, \lnot H \}\), then
\[P(d) = P(d \land H) + P(d \land \lnot H) = P(H)P(d\vert H) + P(\lnot H)P(d\vert \lnot H),\]
where the final step comes from the definition of conditional probability.

title: 9  Bayes’ theorem and the weight of evidence
section: 9.3 The odds form: prior odds, likelihood ratio, posterior odds
text:
9.3 The odds form: prior odds, likelihood ratio, posterior odds
The normalising constant \(P(d)\) is the same for every hypothesis in the hypothesis space, which is the source of a great simplification. Write Bayes’ theorem for two hypotheses, \(H_1\) and \(H_2\), and divide one by the other. The \(P(d)\) cancels:
\[\underbrace{\frac{P(H_1\vert d)}{P(H_2\vert d)}}_{\text{posterior odds}}
= \underbrace{\frac{P(H_1)}{P(H_2)}}_{\text{prior odds}}
   \times
   \underbrace{\frac{P(d\vert H_1)}{P(d\vert H_2)}}_{\text{likelihood ratio}}.\]
In words: posterior odds = prior odds × likelihood ratio. This is Bayes’ theorem in its most useful form. It separates cleanly into the two ingredients of an inference — the prior odds, which carry everything known before the data, and the likelihood ratio, which carries everything the data contribute. The likelihood ratio (for two simple hypotheses, the Bayes factor) is the multiplicative factor by which the data shift the odds. It is the quantitative form of the weak syllogism from Chapter 8: evidence is not “for” a hypothesis in isolation but always relative to a named alternative.
Three consequences follow immediately, and each is a recurring theme of the book:

Evidence is comparative. \(P(d\vert H_1)\) on its own moves nothing; only its ratio to \(P(d\vert H_2)\) does. A hypothesis can be confirmed only against a stated rival.
A small likelihood ratio cannot rescue a small prior, and a large prior cannot be ignored. Both factors multiply.
The prior is unavoidable. Refusing to state one does not remove it; it only hides the prior odds you have implicitly assumed.

9  Bayes' theorem and the weight of evidence

title: 9  Bayes’ theorem and the weight of evidence
text:
9.4 The weight of evidence
Multiplying odds across several independent pieces of evidence is awkward. Taking logarithms turns the product into a sum. Define the weight of evidence as the logarithm of the likelihood ratio,
\[W = \log \frac{P(d\vert H_1)}{P(d\vert H_2)},\]
so that Bayes’ theorem in odds form becomes additive:
\[\log(\text{posterior odds}) = \log(\text{prior odds}) + W.\]
Evidence now behaves like a physical quantity that accumulates: two independent experiments contribute weights \(W_1\) and \(W_2\), and the total evidence is \(W_1 + W_2\). This formulation, and the term “weight of evidence”, are due to I. J. Good, building on wartime work with Alan Turing; in base-ten logarithms the unit is the ban, and one tenth of a ban is the deciban, the smallest change in the plausibility of a hypothesis a person can reasonably perceive.1 Positive weight favours \(H_1\), negative weight favours \(H_2\), and zero weight (likelihood ratio 1) is data that cannot tell the two hypotheses apart — a case that returns, decisively, in the Madame Marie example below. The weight of evidence is also what makes “informative” precise in the card-selection task of Chapter 3: the observation worth making is the one whose expected weight of evidence, averaged over what it might show, is largest.

section: 9.5 A worked example: a diagnostic test
text:
9.5 A worked example: a diagnostic test
(The numbers are of the kind reported for the first antibody tests in the spring of 2020.) We have an antibody test for COVID-19. If 1000 COVID-19 positive patients are tested, on average 840 of them get a true-positive result (sensitivity 84%). If 1000 non-infected people are tested, 5 get a false-positive result (specificity \(1 - 0.005 = 0.995\), or 99.5%). About 1% of the population has been exposed to the virus. If a random person tests positive, what is the probability that this person is infected?

the hypothesis space has two members: \(H_1\) — infected, \(H_2\) — not infected;
priors: \(P(H_1) = 0.01\), \(P(H_2) = 1 - P(H_1) = 0.99\);
likelihoods: \(P(+ \vert H_1) = 0.84\) (sensitivity), \(P(+ \vert H_2) = 0.005\) (1 − specificity).



Show code
Pr_H1 <- 0.01
Pr_H2 <- 1 - Pr_H1
L_H1  <- 0.84
L_H2  <- 0.005
(Pr_infected <- (Pr_H1 * L_H1) / (Pr_H1 * L_H1 + Pr_H2 * L_H2))


[1] 0.6292135


The odds form makes the same calculation transparent. The prior odds of infection are \(0.01 / 0.99 \approx 1\!:\!99\). The likelihood ratio of a positive test — the diagnostic likelihood ratio — is sensitivity over one-minus-specificity:


Show code
prior_odds <- Pr_H1 / Pr_H2
LR_pos     <- L_H1 / L_H2          # = 0.84 / 0.005
post_odds  <- prior_odds * LR_pos
c(LR = LR_pos, weight_of_evidence_bans = log10(LR_pos),
  posterior_odds = post_odds,
  posterior_prob = post_odds / (1 + post_odds))


                     LR weight_of_evidence_bans          posterior_odds 
            168.0000000               2.2253093               1.6969697 
         posterior_prob 
              0.6292135 


A positive result carries a likelihood ratio of 168 — strong evidence, 2.2 bans. Yet because the prior odds are so low (the disease is rare), the posterior probability of infection is only 0.63: the strong evidence multiplies a small prior. This is the base-rate point of Chapter 2, now quantified, and it is also the diagnostic exercise of Chapter 3 completed: with sensitivity 1 a negative test would refute infection outright by the strong syllogism, while with sensitivity 0.84 a positive test only raises its plausibility, by a factor the likelihood ratio now states.
There is a more intuitive route to the same number. Imagine 1000 random persons, 10 of whom are infected and 990 not. Of the infected, \(10 \times 0.84 = 8.4\) test positive; of the uninfected, \(990 \times 0.005 = 5\) test positive. The probability of being infected given a positive test is then \(8.4 / (8.4 + 5) = 0.63\).






The Infectious Diseases Society of America made the practical version of this point in its 2020 guideline on antibody testing.2 Population surveys should use “assays with high specificity (ie, ≥99.5%)”, above all where prevalence is expected to be low, because with an IgA assay of the day and a prevalence of 1%, the panel calculated that about nine in ten positive results would be false positives; and testing individuals was recommended only where clinical suspicion was already high — that is, where the prior odds were no longer small. A rare condition demands a very high likelihood ratio before a positive result means much for an individual.

title: 9  Bayes’ theorem and the weight of evidence
section: 9.6 A worked example: Madame Marie and the hypothesis space
text:
9.6 A worked example: Madame Marie and the hypothesis space
The previous chapter, Chapter 8, introduced the hypothesis space and showed, with a trick coin, that the same data can support opposite headline conclusions in different spaces. This example develops that point with the full odds-form machinery, on a question with a longer pedigree.
Suppose we want to find out whether Madame Marie has extra-sensory perception (ESP). We use a deck of cards bearing one of five symbols, so that pure guessing succeeds with probability \(0.2\), and we record her guesses on \(n = 100\) cards. She gets \(k = 30\) correct — well above the 20 expected by chance.
A frequentist analysis compares this with the hypothesis of pure guessing alone and reports a small p value: 30 or more correct is unlikely if she were guessing at random.


Show code
n <- 100; k <- 30
p_value <- pbinom(k - 1, n, 0.2, lower.tail = FALSE)  # P(X >= 30 | random)
p_value


[1] 0.01124898


The data are indeed inconsistent with pure randomness. But “inconsistent with randomness” is not “evidence for ESP”, because the p value addresses only one hypothesis. Bayes’ theorem forces us to name the alternatives and their likelihoods. Consider three:

\(H_1\) — ESP: she perceives the card, raising her hit rate to, say, \(0.30\);
\(H_2\) — random guessing: hit rate \(0.20\);
\(H_3\) — bias: subtle cues, marked cards, or fraud also raise her hit rate to about \(0.30\).

The likelihoods are binomial (Chapter 7), and the two analyses — the naive two-hypothesis space \(\{H_1, H_2\}\) and the fuller \(\{H_1, H_2, H_3\}\) — differ only in which hypotheses are admitted and what priors they carry:


Show code
L1 <- dbinom(k, n, 0.30)   # ESP
L2 <- dbinom(k, n, 0.20)   # random
L3 <- dbinom(k, n, 0.30)   # bias: same hit rate as ESP

## Naive two-hypothesis space, generously agnostic between ESP and chance
prior2 <- c(ESP = 0.5, random = 0.5)
post2  <- prior2 * c(L1, L2)
post2  <- post2 / sum(post2)

## Fuller space: ESP a priori near-impossible; bias as plausible as chance
prior3 <- c(ESP = 1e-6, random = 0.5, bias = 0.5 - 1e-6)
post3  <- prior3 * c(L1, L2, L3)
post3  <- post3 / sum(post3)

list(LR_ESP_vs_random = L1 / L2,
     LR_ESP_vs_bias   = L1 / L3,
     posterior_2hyp   = round(post2, 4),
     posterior_3hyp_ESP = signif(post3["ESP"], 3))


$LR_ESP_vs_random
[1] 16.72251

$LR_ESP_vs_bias
[1] 1

$posterior_2hyp
   ESP random 
0.9436 0.0564 

$posterior_3hyp_ESP
     ESP 
1.89e-06 


Two things stand out. First, the likelihood ratio of ESP against random guessing is large, so in the naive two-hypothesis space the posterior probability of ESP comes out high — 0.94 — the same impression the small p value gives. Second, the likelihood ratio of ESP against bias is exactly 1: the data fit fraud precisely as well as they fit ESP, and so provide no evidence whatever to choose between them. Once \(H_3\) is admitted — and bias is, a priori, vastly more plausible than ESP — the posterior probability of ESP collapses to \(1.9 \times 10^{-6}\). It has barely moved from its prior of \(10^{-6}\): the data did discredit random guessing, and ESP inherits a sliver of the mass that guessing lost, but almost all of it goes to bias, which the data cannot tell from ESP. The data never bore on the question that matters.
The same data, the same likelihoods for ESP, two opposite conclusions: the difference is entirely in how the hypothesis space was sliced. This is the practical lesson. A p value, comparing the data with a single null, can reject “pure randomness” while saying nothing about ESP versus bias — which is the comparison a scientist actually cares about. Evidence is comparative, and a relevant hypothesis left out of the space can invalidate the whole inference.

9  Bayes' theorem and the weight of evidence

title: 9  Bayes’ theorem and the weight of evidence
text:
9.7 Many hypotheses, and continuous parameters
More generally, for a hypothesis space with \(n\) mutually exclusive and exhaustive hypotheses \(\mathcal{H} = \{H_1, H_2, \dots, H_n\}\),
\[P(d) = P(H_1)P(d\vert H_1) + P(H_2)P(d\vert H_2) + \dots + P(H_n)P(d\vert H_n).\]
This is the formula for total (a.k.a. marginal) probability, and Bayes’ theorem becomes
\[P(H_1\vert d) =\frac{P(H_1)P(d\vert H_1)}{P(H_1)P(d\vert H_1) + P(H_2)P(d \vert H_2) + \dots + P(H_n)P(d \vert H_n)}.\]
What if we want to estimate a continuous parameter — Madame Marie’s true hit rate \(\theta\), the probability that a patient dies of COVID-19, the mean length of a hospital stay? Then the hypothesis space has infinitely many members (every real number from 0 to 1, say), and the prior and the likelihood must be specified for all of them at once. Continuous functions do this: prior and likelihood become probability distributions of the kind catalogued in Chapter 7, the sum in the denominator becomes an integral, and the posterior is a continuous distribution too.
The cleanest case is the beta–binomial conjugacy promised in Chapter 7. Take Marie’s hit rate \(\theta\) as the unknown, put a uniform \(\text{Beta}(1,1)\) prior on it — every hit rate equally plausible before the cards are turned — and use the binomial likelihood of 30 hits in 100. Multiplying a \(\text{Beta}(\alpha,\beta)\) prior by a binomial likelihood with \(s\) successes and \(f\) failures gives a \(\text{Beta}(\alpha+s,\beta+f)\) posterior, with no integral to compute (Figure 9.1).


Show code
theta  <- seq(0, 1, by = 0.001)
a0 <- 1; b0 <- 1                       # uniform prior
post_a <- a0 + k; post_b <- b0 + (n - k)  # conjugate update
lik <- dbinom(k, n, theta)
lik <- lik / max(lik) * max(dbeta(theta, post_a, post_b))
tibble(theta,
       prior      = dbeta(theta, a0, b0),
       likelihood = lik,
       posterior  = dbeta(theta, post_a, post_b)) %>%
  pivot_longer(-theta) %>%
  mutate(name = factor(name, levels = c("prior", "likelihood", "posterior"))) %>%
  ggplot(aes(theta, value, colour = name)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
  labs(x = expression(theta ~ "(hit rate)"), y = "density", colour = NULL)








Figure 9.1: Madame Marie’s hit rate as a continuous parameter. A uniform Beta(1, 1) prior and 30 hits in 100 cards give a Beta(31, 71) posterior; the likelihood is rescaled to the posterior’s height for display.





The posterior is \(\text{Beta}(31, 71)\): its mean is 0.30, and 95% of its mass lies between 0.22 and 0.40 — the interval summary that Chapter 10 names the credible interval and develops. Notice what this analysis does and does not say. It estimates how often Marie hits, and finds the rate well above 0.2; it is silent on why, because a hit rate is not a hypothesis about ESP versus bias. The continuous parameter has replaced the discrete hypothesis space, and the question the three-hypothesis space made explicit has disappeared back into the choice of what to model. When no conjugate shortcut exists, the posterior is obtained numerically; the grid approximation of Chapter 10 is the most direct method, and Markov chain Monte Carlo (Section 23.2.2) the general one.

title: 9  Bayes’ theorem and the weight of evidence
section: 9.8 Updating, exchangeability, and what Bayes does not guarantee
text:
9.8 Updating, exchangeability, and what Bayes does not guarantee
Bayes’ theorem combines, in the logically optimal way, the evidence in the data (through the likelihood) with the data-independent beliefs (through the prior), and returns a posterior. There is no magic involved, just probability theory. Bayes’ theorem is not a truth machine — it combines the information put into it. If the prior or the likelihood is grossly wrong, there is no guarantee that the posterior converges on the truth, even in the long run (although under most realistic conditions it does).
Two practical properties follow. First, the theorem works iteratively, and with no lower limit on the data: \(N = 1\) is fine.3 Yesterday’s posterior becomes today’s prior, new data enter as a new likelihood, and the updated posterior in turn becomes tomorrow’s prior; because the product rule does not care how the data are grouped, updating on a hundred observations one at a time gives the same posterior as updating on all hundred at once. Bayesian inference thereby recapitulates the piecemeal nature of scientific inference, and because evidence is additive on the log scale (the weight-of-evidence section), accumulating studies is addition. One consequence is that nothing stops an analyst computing the posterior after every new observation. The frequentist concern with stopping rules arises from the need to control long-run error rates and has no counterpart here — a contrast that Chapter 10 opens with and the significance-chasing section of Appendix G spells out.
Second, the data need not be independent draws from a fixed population. What the analysis requires is that they be exchangeable: that the joint probability of the observations be unchanged by reordering them, so that their order carries no information (Chapter 8). De Finetti’s representation theorem, met in that chapter, is what makes exchangeability enough: an exchangeable sequence is mathematically a sequence that is independent and identically distributed (iid; independence was defined in Chapter 6) given an unknown parameter, with a prior over that parameter — exactly the structure prior × likelihood assumes. The iid assumption of a frequentist analysis and the exchangeability judgement of a Bayesian one are therefore the same judgement about the data, made unconditionally in the first case and conditionally on the parameter in the second; what the Bayesian gains is the freedom to put a distribution on the unknown rather than treat it as fixed. Where the observations are not exchangeable — measurements ordered in time, patients clustered within hospitals — the model must say how they depend on one another, which is the work of Part V.
crumbs: Part II. Probability is the logic of science
9  Bayes' theorem and the weight of evidence

title: 9  Bayes’ theorem and the weight of evidence
text:
9.9 Where this leads
The theorem is in hand, in three forms: the direct form, the odds form, and the additive log form. What it has not yet done is compute a posterior that no conjugate pair hands over for free; Chapter 10 does that with the grid approximation, and states the credible interval that this chapter’s beta–binomial example only gestured at. The p value, which this chapter used only as a foil, is set out with its problems in Appendix G. And the point on which everything here has turned — that evidence is comparative, and that a hypothesis left out of the space cannot be revived by any data — returns in Part III, where the hypotheses are causal structures and the omitted one is usually a confounder.
crumbs: Part II. Probability is the logic of science
9  Bayes' theorem and the weight of evidence

title: 9  Bayes’ theorem and the weight of evidence
text:
9.10 Key points

Bayes’ theorem combines prior and likelihood into a posterior: \(P(H\vert d) \propto P(H)\,P(d\vert H)\). The denominator \(P(d)\) only normalises.
In odds form, posterior odds = prior odds × likelihood ratio. The \(P(d)\) cancels, separating the inference into what was known before (prior odds) and what the data contribute (the likelihood ratio, a.k.a. the Bayes factor for simple hypotheses).
The weight of evidence is the logarithm of the likelihood ratio; on the log scale Bayes’ theorem is additive, so independent studies sum. Positive weight favours \(H_1\), negative \(H_2\); zero weight is data that cannot tell them apart.
Evidence is comparative: a likelihood addresses a hypothesis only relative to a named alternative. A likelihood ratio of 1 is no evidence, whatever the p value says.
A rare condition (low prior) needs a large likelihood ratio before a positive test means much — the base-rate point, quantified (the diagnostic example).
For a continuous parameter the hypothesis space is a distribution; with a conjugate pair (beta prior, binomial data) the posterior is arithmetic on the parameters. Estimating a rate is not the same question as choosing between explanations of it.
How the hypothesis space is sliced determines the conclusion. A p value compares the data with a single null and is silent on the comparison that matters; omitting a plausible hypothesis (bias, in the ESP example) can invalidate the inference.
Bayes’ theorem updates iteratively, with no minimum \(N\) and no need for stopping rules, and requires the data to be exchangeable — by de Finetti’s theorem, iid given the parameter. It is not a truth machine: rubbish in, rubbish out.

title: 9  Bayes’ theorem and the weight of evidence
text:
9.11 Exercises

Odds form by hand. Repeat the diagnostic-test calculation for a population where the base rate is 10% rather than 1%, keeping the same sensitivity and specificity. Compute the posterior probability of infection both ways (direct Bayes and odds form), and report the weight of evidence of a positive test in bans. Why does the posterior change even though the likelihood ratio does not?
Evidence adds up. A patient takes the antibody test twice, independently, and both results are positive. Using the weight-of- evidence formula, add the two weights and convert back to a posterior probability (start from the 1% prior). Confirm the result by applying Bayes’ theorem twice, using the first posterior as the second prior.
Re-slice the deck. In the Madame Marie code, change Marie’s score to \(k = 45\) and re-run both analyses. Does the larger likelihood ratio against randomness change the three-hypothesis conclusion about ESP? Explain why or why not in terms of the likelihood ratio of ESP against bias.
Make bias implausible. Suppose the experiment is run under conditions that make fraud and cueing nearly impossible, so that the prior on \(H_3\) falls to \(10^{-4}\) while the prior on ESP stays at \(10^{-6}\). Recompute the three-hypothesis posterior for ESP. What does this tell you about where the real work of an ESP experiment lies — in the data or in the design?
From the cohort. Source R/simulate_cohort.R and generate the cohort. Estimate the stroke risk among treated and untreated patients, \(P(\text{stroke}\vert\text{drug})\) and \(P(\text{stroke}\vert\lnot\text{drug})\), by counting. Treat these as likelihoods and take a prior of 0.5 that a randomly chosen patient was treated; update on “this patient had a stroke” to obtain \(P(\text{drug}\vert\text{stroke})\). Explain why this posterior is an associational quantity and must not be read as the effect of the drug (Chapter 4 and Chapter 11).
Conceptual: the single null. A colleague reports “p = 0.001, so the effect is real.” Using the odds form and the ESP example, explain in a short paragraph what is missing from this inference and what additional quantities would be needed to make it.
A sceptical conjugate prior. Repeat the beta–binomial update of Marie’s hit rate with a \(\text{Beta}(4, 16)\) prior, which is centred on the chance rate of 0.2 and worth about 20 cards of information. Compare the two posteriors’ means and 95% intervals. How many cards, at the observed hit rate of 0.3, would it take before the uniform and the sceptical prior give posterior means within 0.01 of each other?

title: 10  Bayesian inference in practice
text:
10.1 Two workflows
Side by side, Table 10.1 sets out the two traditions’ typical procedures.
The frequentist discipline exists to control long-run error rates. Dichotomising continuous evidence at a significance threshold creates the multiple-testing problem,2 and only pre-registration keeps researcher degrees of freedom from destroying the error control that the tests promise; the price is an analysis that cannot react to results it did not anticipate. It would be a mistake to suppose that these requirements, which come from the need to fix the long-run frequency of type I errors, describe how scientists reason.
The Bayesian analysis needs no stopping rule and no pre-specified test, because there is no significance level to protect and the posterior is a valid summary at any \(N\). What it needs instead is an explicit model, and its checks are checks of that model: simulated data before fitting (the prior predictive check) and after (the posterior predictive check), both met below and made routine in Chapter 23. Both traditions want the same thing — scientific conclusions drawn from fitted models, which have to be interpreted outside the mathematics — and differ in how much of the reasoning they make explicit. One difference of substance: the Bayesian interprets all the effects in a model together, because the principle of total information (desideratum 3.2 of Chapter 8) forbids discarding evidence, whereas the habit of interpreting only significant effects — an historical accident, not a requirement of frequentist theory — discards most of it.
crumbs: Part II. Probability is the logic of science

title: 10  Bayesian inference in practice
text:
Table 10.1: The two workflows.










Stage
Frequentist
Bayesian




Before the data
Pre-register the stopping rule,1 the tests, the variables and their transformations; a power analysis fixes the sample size \(N\)
Choose a data model (the likelihood) and priors; simulate data from them to see what they imply and whether the fitting procedure copes — which doubles as a power analysis


Collecting
Exactly \(N\) observations, analysed together; no peeking unless pre-specified; randomised and blinded where possible
Randomised and blinded where possible; no stopping rule is needed, and the posterior may be updated as the data arrive (Chapter 9)


Fitting
The pre-specified test on the pre-specified variables
Prior × likelihood → posterior; in practice by MCMC rather than by direct calculation (Section 23.2.2)


Checking
Test the assumptions (normality, linearity, constant variance) with further tests on the data and the fitted model
Simulate data from the fitted model and compare with the real data, to see which aspects of the data the model captures and which it misses


Interpreting
Raw effect sizes and p values; one model per effect; in practice, often only the “significant” effects
Posteriors — shrunk estimates (Chapter 23) with credible intervals; all effects together; often several models compared


Iterating
Departures from the protocol are “researcher degrees of freedom” and threaten the error control
Modify the model, refit, repeat until its simulated data resemble the real data; then interpret in scientific context and make counterfactual predictions









Bayesian inference comes straight from probability theory; frequentist inference is a collection of procedures that require more stringent conditions to work properly.

title: 10  Bayesian inference in practice
text:
10.2 The data model
Start with the direction of reasoning that Chapter 7 called modelling the data-generating mechanism: fix the parameter, and ask what data it produces. Suppose the mortality of a disease is 50% and we have 3 patients. How many of them will die? The parameter is fixed at \(p = 0.5\), the sample size at \(N = 3\), and the sample space — the set of possible outcomes — has four members: 0, 1, 2 or 3 deaths. Enumerate every sequence of deaths (d) and survivals (a) that three patients can produce (Table 10.2):



Table 10.2: The eight equally probable futures of three patients when each dies with probability 0.5.





Deaths
Sequences
Count




0
aaa
1


1
daa, ada, aad
3


2
dda, dad, add
3


3
ddd
1






With \(p = 0.5\) every sequence is equally probable, so the \(1 + 3 + 3 + 1 = 8\) futures divide among the four outcomes by counting: \(P(1 \text{ death}) = 3/8\), and so on (Figure 10.1).


Show code
x <- 0:3
p_count <- tibble(x, y = c(1, 3, 3, 1)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x, y)) + geom_point() + geom_line() +
  labs(x = "number of deaths", y = "number of sequences")
p_binom <- tibble(x, y = dbinom(x, 3, 0.5)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x, y)) + geom_point() + geom_line() +
  labs(x = "number of deaths", y = "probability")
p_count + p_binom








Figure 10.1: Three patients, mortality 0.5. Left: the number of sequences producing each count of deaths. Right: the same distribution normalised, from the binomial model.





One death and two deaths are equally likely, and each is three times as likely as no deaths or three deaths. The right panel is the binomial distribution of Chapter 7 doing the counting for us: dbinom(x, 3, 0.5) returns, for each possible number of deaths \(x\), its probability given the fixed mortality. For 9 patients and a mortality of 67% the same call gives Figure 10.2.


Show code
x <- 0:9
tibble(x, y = dbinom(x, 9, 0.67)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x, y)) + geom_point() + geom_line() +
  labs(x = "number of deaths", y = "probability")








Figure 10.2: Nine patients, mortality 0.67: the binomial probability of each number of deaths.





This is the data model, or sampling distribution: with the parameter fixed, it assigns a probability to every dataset that might be observed, and the probabilities sum to one over the sample space. It is not yet a likelihood, and there is no prior and no posterior in it — a prior is a distribution over parameters, and here the parameter is known. What turns the data model into a likelihood is a shift of perspective: hold the data fixed and let the parameter vary.

title: 10  Bayesian inference in practice
text:
10.3 Fitting the binomial data model
We observe 6 deaths among 9 patients and want to estimate the true mortality rate.

data: 6 dead out of 9 patients;
parameter to estimate: the mortality rate \(p\);
parameter space — the hypothesis space of Chapter 8 — every real number between 0 and 1.

The same dbinom() serves. It has three arguments — number of events, number of trials, and probability of an event — and before, two of them were fixed and the third was the outcome; now the two data values are fixed and the probability is the unknown. Read this way, dbinom(6, 9, p) as a function of \(p\) is the likelihood: it does not sum to one over \(p\) (Chapter 9), and it is the data’s verdict on each candidate value. We use a flat prior. As the parameter space has infinitely many members, we cheat a little and evaluate prior and likelihood on a grid of 20 evenly spaced values (Figure 10.3).


Show code
# grid: mortality at 20 evenly spaced probabilities from 0 to 1
x <- seq(from = 0, to = 1, length.out = 20)
prior <- rep(1, 20)                       # flat prior
likelihood <- dbinom(6, size = 9, prob = x)  # likelihood at each grid value
posterior <- likelihood * prior / sum(likelihood * prior)

tibble(x = rep(x, 2),
       y = c(likelihood, posterior),
       curve = rep(c("likelihood", "posterior"), each = 20)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x, y, colour = curve)) +
  geom_line() +
  labs(x = "mortality p", y = NULL, colour = NULL)








Figure 10.3: Six deaths in nine patients on a 20-point grid: the binomial likelihood and the posterior under a flat prior. The posterior is the likelihood rescaled to sum to one.





The posterior sums to one; with a flat prior its shape is that of the likelihood, rescaled.
Now do the same one patient at a time, so that each update uses \(n = 1\) — the iterative updating of Chapter 9 made visible. The first patient died (Figure 10.4).


Show code
likelihood <- dbinom(1, size = 1, prob = x)
posterior <- likelihood * prior / sum(likelihood * prior)
tibble(x, posterior) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x, posterior)) + geom_line(colour = "blue") +
  labs(x = "mortality p", y = "posterior")








Figure 10.4: After one patient, who died: the posterior under a flat prior.





Zero mortality is now logically impossible and 100 percent mortality is the hypothesis best supported by the data.
The second patient also died. The previous posterior is now the prior (Figure 10.5).


Show code
prior <- posterior
likelihood <- dbinom(1, size = 1, prob = x)
posterior1 <- likelihood * prior / sum(likelihood * prior)
tibble(x, prior, posterior1) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x)) + geom_line(aes(y = prior)) +
  geom_line(aes(y = posterior1), colour = "blue") +
  labs(x = "mortality p", y = "probability")








Figure 10.5: After two patients, both of whom died: the previous posterior (black) serves as prior; the new posterior is in blue.





The posterior is no longer a straight line. 100 percent mortality is still the most likely mortality estimate.
The third patient survived (Figure 10.6).


Show code
prior <- posterior1
likelihood <- dbinom(0, size = 1, prob = x)
posterior2 <- likelihood * prior / sum(likelihood * prior)
tibble(x, prior, posterior2) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x)) + geom_line(aes(y = prior)) +
  geom_line(aes(y = posterior2), colour = "blue") +
  labs(x = "mortality p", y = "probability")








Figure 10.6: After three patients (died, died, survived): prior in black, posterior in blue.





Now zero mortality and 100 percent mortality are both logically impossible. The posterior peaks at a mortality of \(2/3\) — on our coarse grid, at 0.68 — which is also the raw proportion, as it must be under a flat prior. Updating in a different order, or on all three patients at once, gives the same curve (Exercise 2).
