title: Appendix G — Null hypothesis testing
text:
G.1 A drug trial and two explanations
You are working in a drug company, which has just conducted a randomised controlled study (RCT) on a prospective blood pressure drug and found that it reduces mean systolic BP by 2 mmHg, compared to placebo (“mm” below). Because these results come from a finite random sample, although they could point to a real effect, they could also result from sampling error, which simply means that due to pure chance the group of people on the drug and the group on placebo happen to be different in ways that lead to some non-zero difference (effect size) regardless of the causal action of the drug.
There are two possibilities that could explain your result. (i) The drug group has lower BP, because the drug lowered it, (ii) It has lower BP completely randomly (for example if, accidentally, the people in the drug group were with lower BP to begin with, then it makes sense that they ended up with lower BP after taking the drug, even if the drug has no effect on BP).
The next step is to state that in case our results can be readily explained by sampling error, we will not give credence to the hypothesis that it was the drug that caused the observed 2 mm effect. But how do we know, whether our results are consistent with the sampling effect hypothesis? For this we need to model effect sizes (i) under a specific hypothesis of no drug effect at all and (ii) have an idea of how such effect might be distributed.
What comes out of this is a method called null hypothesis testing, which compares your statistic with a whole distribution of model-generated statistics. If your effect, which was calculated in the clinical study, is similar enough to effects which are expected to occur even if the drug does not work, then you can conclude exactly nothing. On the other hand, if your effect is unlikely under the null hypothesis of no drug effect, then you have a choice of either being surprised, because you just saw something unlikely, or alternatively, you can conclude that there must be something other than the random sampling error that caused your 2 mm effect. So which road should you take, the road of surprise or the road of happiness? That depends on what you know of your drug candidate. If there is independent reason to believe that similar drugs might be reasonably effective, then acceptance that you have made a discovery, is a good choice. On the other hand, should you later learn that your compound was actually degraded and could not have the supposed biological effect, then you might as well go with the surprise.
What happens, if your study is not an RCT, but based on observational data? Now, obviously, you do not have randomisation and thus randomised data. And yet you will model your statistic under the null hypothesis, as if it came from randomised experiments. This is because you do not know, how to do it any differently! But do not lose hope (at least not yet), because there is a remedy. If you can perfectly match your groups so that the result is practically identical to randomisation, then you are good to go. For this you need a full causal framework to decide on which variables to match your sample. If you cannot do this, then you can still calculate null hypothesis tests, as many people do – only know that the p value then speaks to sampling error alone, and says nothing about the confounding that Part III is about.
Figure G.1: From data to a sampling distribution, and where the p value lives. Panel A shows the data distribution: the blood-pressure change of each of the n = 100 individual patients in a single sample. The data are widely spread, and this spread is summarised by the standard deviation (SD = 10 mm). The red line marks the one number we actually care about, the sample mean effect of 2 mm. Panel B shows a different distribution entirely: the sampling distribution of the mean – the distribution of mean effects we would expect to see if we repeated the whole study many times and the point null hypothesis were true (H0: the drug’s true effect is exactly 0 mm, dashed line). This distribution is centred on the H0 value of 0, and its width is not the SD of the data but the standard error of the mean, SEM = SD/sqrt(n) = 10/sqrt(100) = 1 mm. Averaging over 100 patients makes the sampling distribution ten times narrower than the data distribution – this is why a 2 mm mean can sit far out in the tail even though individual patients vary by tens of mm. The p value is the red shaded area: the probability, if H0 were true, of getting a sample mean at least as extreme as the 2 mm we observed (both tails, +/- 2 mm). Here p = 0.046. A small p value does not say the drug works; it only says that a result like ours would be uncommon in a world where the drug does nothing.

title: Appendix G — Null hypothesis testing
section: G.2 The sampling distribution and the central limit theorem
text:
G.2 The sampling distribution and the central limit theorem
The device that made Figure G.1 possible is the sampling distribution: the distribution a statistic would have over imagined repetitions of the study. It is what carries the frequencies in this framework. Imagine an infinite population of measurement values, from which we draw a random and independent sample of \(N\) values and compute the mean. The sample mean reflects the population mean, but not precisely; the discrepancy is sampling error, and it shrinks with the square root of \(N\), so that each halving of the error costs four times the data. The standard deviation of the sample mean over repetitions is the standard error of the mean, \(\text{SEM} = \sigma/\sqrt{N}\). Because \(\sigma\) is unknown it is estimated by the sample SD, and when \(N\) is small that estimate is poor, which is why the classical tests use Student’s t distribution with \(N - 1\) degrees of freedom in place of the normal (Chapter 7): the t has the heavier tails that an estimated SEM deserves, and converges to the normal as \(N\) grows. Sums of squared standard-normal deviations follow the chi-squared distribution exactly, which is why that distribution governs the classical tests on variances and on contingency tables (Chapter 7).
Why the sampling distribution of a mean is so often normal, whatever the data look like, is the central limit theorem, stated in Chapter 7: the mean of \(N\) independent draws from any distribution with finite variance approaches a normal distribution as \(N\) grows. The theorem is a limit statement; it names no sample size. The rule of thumb “N at least 30” is folklore, and Figure G.2 shows a skewed parent for which it fails: 1 000 samples of size 3, 10, 30 and 100 from a standard log-normal distribution, whose means are still visibly right-skewed at \(N = 30\).








Figure G.2: The central limit theorem on a skewed parent. Density of the means of 1 000 samples of size 3, 10, 30 and 100 drawn from a standard log-normal distribution, with the raw data (dashed). The means of 30 are still right-skewed; the approach to the normal is gradual and depends on the parent.









Table G.1: Skewness of the raw log-normal data and of the sample means at each sample size (a normal distribution has skewness 0).

The table, Table G.1, puts numbers on the picture: the skewness of the means falls roughly as \(1/\sqrt{N}\) and is still 0.9 at \(N = 30\), against 5.5 for the raw data and 0 for a normal; at \(N = 100\) it is 0.6. How large \(N\) must be depends on how skewed the parent is, and a rule that ignores the parent is not a rule.

title: Appendix G — Null hypothesis testing
text:
G.3 Null hypothesis (H0)
The null hypothesis (H0) is a technical term that usually defines a treatment effect that is completely missing. For example, if the actual Risk Difference (RD) in the population, which is not the same RD that was estimated by the researcher, is exactly zero, and the corresponding Risk Ratio (RR) is exactly one, then we can say “the null hypothesis holds” or “the null is true”. As we can never prove on data that a given null hypothesis holds, we use the H0 as a conceptual aid in testing our data against a rather abstract hypothesis of exactly null effect.
This is the point null hypothesis, so-called because it covers a point value in the continuous scale. However, the sampling distribution generated from this point null generally takes the form of a continuous distribution, like the normal distribution shown above. This creates some ambiguity, when people talk about their sample statistic “under” the null hypothesis.
First, one could argue that the underlying point null is ill-defined, as in real life there are (practically) no true null effects. In biology, at least, meaningful experimental treatments tend to always lead to some non-null effect, however tiny. Seen like this, null hypothesis testing is an abstract mathematical invention looking for an adequate use case – despite being the most widely used statistical method in the 20th century!
On the other hand, it could also be argued that as in testing the null we are actually testing our sample data-derived effect size against the sampling distribution of effect sizes under the null, this allows us to filter out effects that are large enough to come through the statistical significance filter. So we don’t have to worry about “true nulls” being exactly null, as long as the power of our study is just about right to find the scientifically interesting effects and filter out the ones that are too small to matter. However, which effects are large enough to pass the filter is largely determined by the sample size (the right N is estimated by power calculations). It then follows that should you accept this view of the null hypothesis, then you only want to use the method after a successful power analysis. No power calculation – no reason to think that statistical significance filters out the right effects – therefore no reason to do H0 testing.

title: Appendix G — Null hypothesis testing
text:
G.4 P values
The main output of any null hypothesis test is the p value. This is the measure of how similar your data are to the data that might appear randomly if your experimental treatment actually has no effect on the outcome. A large p value is taken to mean good correspondence between your data and the null hypothesis. A good correspondence with the null does not mean that your data suggest no treatment effect. It merely tells you that a possible real effect was not identified by your data. It is possible that had you collected more data, or had your random sample been a little different, you might have well seen the true effect that for now eludes you.

P value is the probability of encountering your sample data or more extreme data, if we suppose that there really is no effect.

P value is in the probability scale (0…1) and it tries to answer the question of how likely it is to see data like yours, assuming that there is actually no true effect. A p value says nothing about the likelihood that the effect, which you see, might be biased (unless you have done a perfect RCT or perfect matching) and it says very little about the actual size of your effect. Most importantly, p value does not give the probability that there is no effect (that the null hypothesis is true), and neither gives it the probability that some scientifically interesting hypothesis is true or false. Thus the direct interpretative use of a raw p value is quite limited.4
The logic, stated in three steps, is this. First, as hypotheses have no probabilities but datasets do, we can speak of the probability of the data under a hypothesis, \(P(d \mid h)\), in the hope that it says something about the hypothesis; for a two-group comparison the natural hypothesis to condition on is the null, \(H_0\), under which the two group means are identical. Second, even if there is no effect, sampling error produces one, equally likely in either direction, and any true effect sits on top of it; if the observed effect is not much larger than the sampling error the two cannot be disentangled without new data, and if it is much larger we may call it non-random – which in no way guarantees that the experimental treatment caused it. Third, the sampling error under \(H_0\) is modelled as the sampling distribution of the previous section, centred on zero with standard deviation SEM, and the fraction of that distribution cut off beyond the observed mean is the one-sided p value; both tails together give the two-sided p value of Figure G.1. Fisher introduced the p value in this form, as an informal measure of the strength of evidence against \(H_0\): a p of 0.001, he suggested, would rarely be seen if \(H_0\) held.5 The section on the weight of evidence below shows why that intuition overstates the case.

title: Appendix G — Null hypothesis testing
text:
G.5 Statistical significance
Statistical significance is a concept that uses p values as input and converts small p values into action. A decade after Fisher, Neyman and Pearson added the significance level \(\alpha\) and derived a different use for the p value: not a comment on the experiment at hand but a long-run quality control on the experimental system that produced it.6 Their procedure makes discoveries automatically and with fixed error rates: if \(p < \alpha\), the result is declared statistically significant, and by setting \(\alpha\) we fix the long-run relative frequency of type I errors – true nulls classified as significant – at \(\alpha\). The dichotomisation costs information, and it promises a formal procedure for making discoveries with no scientific input beyond the data; if that worked, being a scientist would be a low-education job.

If your p value is less than some arbitrary value, like 0.05, and if you then always claim that your result is “statistically significant”, then in the long run 5% of experiments with zero true effects are classified as “significant”.

The interpretation of “significance” is (i) over the long run, rather than about a specific experiment, and (ii) it depends on the fraction of true null experiments (the ones with zero effect) from all experiments that were done.7
Why use significance level 0.05? Why not 0.01 or even lower? The answer lies in a trade-off, where the lower the probability of obtaining a statistically significant result under true null, the higher the probability of missing out on true effects by labelling them “non-significant”. So the trade-off lies in which kind of error scares you more, fear of missing out vs. fear of false discoveries. As there are no clear instructions on how to solve this, most people prefer to pretend that the historic significance level that worked so well for Ronald Fisher who studied the effects of fertiliser on crop yield in the 1920s, is still good enough for whatever they are studying in the 21st century. For example, which is worse, to label a non-working drug as having a “statistically significant” effect and send it to the next multimillion dollar cycle of clinical studies or burying a working drug forever, because it happened to be “statistically non-significant” in your first low-N study? Obviously, the answer to this one is highly context-dependent.
The Neyman–Pearson procedure is fine, statistically speaking; its use in science carries a danger that depends on what scientists test. With \(\alpha = 0.05\) they agree to publish, on average, every twentieth true null as a significant false positive. How much harm follows depends on the base rate of true effects among the hypotheses tested: if most tested hypotheses are true, the fraction of significant results that are false is small and significance is no obvious folly; if scientists take risks and test hypotheses most of which are false – which philosophers of science agree is what good scientists should do – the same procedure paints a badly misleading picture of a field, because most of its discoveries are false.8








Figure G.3: The Neyman-Pearson decision procedure. Neyman and Pearson turned the p value into an automatic accept/reject rule by pitting two hypotheses against each other. Panel A shows two sampling distributions of the mean effect (same SEM = 1 mm scale as the previous figure): the H0 distribution, centred on no effect, and an H1 distribution, centred on a specific effect we would like to be able to detect (here 2.5 mm). We pick a decision threshold (dashed line) and call any study landing to its right “statistically significant”. The threshold cuts each curve in two, producing four areas. Under H0 the area to the left of the threshold is the specificity (true-negative rate, 1 - alpha = 0.95): how often we correctly stay silent when the drug is inert; the small tail to the right is the type I error rate alpha (false positives, 0.05). Under H1 the area to the right of the threshold is the sensitivity, also called the power (true-positive rate, 0.80): how often we correctly flag a real effect; the area to the left is the type II error rate beta (false negatives, 0.20). Panel B lays the same four outcomes out as a 2x2 table. Note the built-in trade-off: sliding the threshold rightwards shrinks alpha (fewer false alarms, higher specificity) but enlarges beta (more misses, lower sensitivity). Choosing a significance level is therefore choosing where to sit on this trade-off, not discovering a fact about nature.

title: Appendix G — Null hypothesis testing
section: G.6 An example: three RCTs of BP medicine
text:
G.6 An example: three RCTs of BP medicine
You are an executive of a drug company which has conducted RCT-s of three completely independent drug candidates for blood pressure reduction. The average systolic BP for study participants was 160 mm and the trials were drug vs. placebo. All three drugs result in lowering of BP and all give identically statistically significant results.

ES= 2 mm, p=0.045
ES= 10 mm, p=0.045
ES= 20 mm, p=0.045

How do you proceed from here? Which drug(s) should be studied further, which axed, which drug candidate is the most promising of the three? To answer this question we need to use additional information that was not used in the calculation of p value and does not reside in the p value. But first, let’s see how the p value of 0.045 translates into 95% confidence intervals (CI). In the first case, the intervals are really narrow around the estimated effect size of 2 mm. In the second case the CI-s are rather wide and in the third case they are wider still. But what does it mean? To extract meaning from CI-s, we must decide a couple of things.

What is a clinically meaningful effects size? In other words, which effect would be too small to matter in clinical and/or drug development pipeline context? Because there are already many BP drugs on the market, one assumes that the minimal clinically useful value must be a bit lower than a minimally useful value for a drug company. But anyway, let’s define it arbitrarily as 5 mm. This means that our first drug with its 2 mm effect is as good as useless, and the CI-s indicate that we can state this with high confidence. I.e, we have plenty of evidence on which to base our decision to abandon drug no 1.
What is the likely/possible range of drug effects, based on previous experience with similar drugs. Here the published literature is informative: a meta-analysis of 354 placebo-controlled trials put the standard-dose systolic reduction at about 9 mm Hg, rising slightly with baseline pressure to roughly 9.7 mm Hg for a cohort starting at 160 mm.9 We can encode this prior expectation as a normal distribution with a mean of about 10 and a standard deviation of 2.5 (so that effects much above 15 mm are treated as unlikely), or, if we do not want to discount effects over 15 mm too heavily, as a Student’s t distribution with somewhat fat tails (say, nu=3). According to this criterion, the second drug is right where we thought it most likely to see its effect prior to our study. But its CI go deep into clinically uninteresting territory, and on the other side, deep into experimentally unlikely territory. Thus we could conclude that drug 2 is a reasonable candidate for further study, but having said that, we have relatively light evidence of its effect being in the window we aimed for.

How about the third drug? Its most likely estimated effect is way too big under our prior hypothesis of expected effect sizes. This raises suspicion about the design and conduct of the study which resulted in this effect. So any irregularities there should be sussed out. But then, it is also true that the CI-s here are extremely wide, going into territory where the reduction in BP could seriously harm patients. If uncertainty is that wide, given a half-reasonable sample size, this could well mean that actual patients were put to danger during this trial. One more reason to proceed with extreme caution!
In conclusion, the first p=0.045 meant a very tight effect size estimate close to zero; the second p=0.045 meant a potentially interesting drug candidate that needs further study; and the third p=0.045 sent a clear message: Keep away! Danger! These separate meanings do not reside in the p values themselves, which are identical, but in the effect sizes combined with sample sizes, prior expectations and clinical/business windows. Note that any interpretation of an effect size presupposes prior knowledge of the possible, and impossible, effects.








Figure G.4: Same p value, three very different drugs. All three trials are ‘statistically significant’ at p = 0.045, yet putting their effect sizes and 95% confidence intervals on a common millimetre scale tells three different stories. Because the p value is identical, every interval just barely clears zero (left edge near 0 mm); the intervals simply fan out wider as the effect grows, so p alone hides both the size and the precision of the effect. Two reference structures help interpret the estimates. The blue band and top curve are the prior expectation for a standard-dose antihypertensive: a meta-analysis of 354 placebo-controlled trials (Law et al. 2003, BMJ) gives a pooled SBP reduction of about 9 mm, shifted to 9.7 mm for these patients’ 160 mm baseline, with a spread realistic for a new trial (prior approximately Normal with mean 9.7 and SD 2.5 mm; 95% range 4.8-14.6 mm). The green shaded region is an illustrative clinical window: reductions below roughly 5 mm (the dotted MCID line) are too small to matter clinically. Reading the three drugs against these windows: Drug 1 (ES = 2 mm) is significant but its entire interval lies below the clinical threshold and far below prior expectation – a real-looking but clinically trivial result. Drug 2 (ES = 10 mm) sits right inside both the clinical window and the prior – the most credible and promising candidate. Drug 3 (ES = 20 mm) has a point estimate twice the largest effect seen across 354 trials; such an estimate from a single significant study is more likely an over-estimate from a low-powered trial than a genuine super-drug, and its enormous interval reflects how little we really know. The 5 mm clinical threshold is illustrative and can be set to whatever the exercise requires.

title: Appendix G — Null hypothesis testing
section: G.7 Absence of evidence: testing for equivalence
text:
G.7 Absence of evidence: testing for equivalence
A large p value is not evidence that the effect is zero – it is only a failure to rule zero out, and that failure can equally well mean the study was simply too small to see a real effect. So how could you ever provide positive evidence that a drug does not have a clinically meaningful effect: that two formulations are interchangeable, say, or that a cheaper generic is no worse than the original? Ordinary null hypothesis testing cannot do this, because you can never “accept H0”.
The frequentist tool for the job is equivalence testing, most often the two one-sided tests (TOST) procedure.10 You begin by declaring an equivalence margin – the smallest effect that would still matter – which is exactly the clinical threshold (the MCID) we drew on the millimetre scale for the three drugs. Then, instead of testing against zero, you run two one-sided tests against the edges of that margin, and ask whether the effect is significantly above the lower bound AND significantly below the upper bound. If both tests pass, you have positively demonstrated that the effect, whatever its sign, is too small to care about. Equivalence and non-inferiority designs of just this kind are what regulators require before approving a generic drug.
Notice that this is the same machinery as before – one-sided tail probabilities against a null – with the null simply moved off zero to the margin you actually care about. In the estimation framework the rest of this book prefers, you get the same conclusion more directly: compute the interval and check whether it lies entirely inside the equivalence margin. If the whole compatibility interval sits between, say, -5 and +5 mm, the data are telling you the effect is trivially small; if it pokes out past the margin, they are not. TOST is just this interval reading dressed up as two tests.

title: Appendix G — Null hypothesis testing
text:
G.8 P values have problems
Suppose you draw a line by any method (incl. statistical significance) and treat any and all effects that cross it as discoveries, and ignore the effects which failed to cross into “significance”. It makes no difference where you put the line or which method you use to calculate statistical significance – what happens is that while the effect may be on a continuous scale (BP difference in mm, risk difference in percentage points, or whatever), your result will be either “a discovery” or “a non-discovery”. There are a few problems associated with this.

G.8.1 The problem of the love of God
The thing is that two extremely similar effects may happen to land on the opposite sides of the decision line. And yet, in God’s eyes, it is clear that they deserve equal love. Then why not in yours?11








Figure G.5: The difference between ‘significant’ and ‘not significant’ is not itself significant. Panel A shows two drug effects, each judged separately against the null of zero. Drug A (6 mm, SE 2) is comfortably ‘significant’ (p = 0.003, its interval excludes zero); Drug B (3 mm, SE 2) is ‘not significant’ (p = 0.13, its interval includes zero). It is tempting to conclude that the two drugs behave differently – one works, the other does not. Panel B tests that conclusion directly by estimating the difference between the two effects (6 - 3 = 3 mm, with SE = sqrt(2^2 + 2^2) = 2.8). That difference is not significant (p = 0.29): its interval comfortably includes zero. So the data do not actually show that Drug A and Drug B differ. The lesson (Gelman & Stern 2006) is that you cannot compare two effects by checking whether each one separately crosses the significance line; whether two estimates differ is a separate question that requires its own test of their difference. Two effects can sit on opposite sides of the significance threshold and still be statistically indistinguishable from one another.







G.8.2 The problem of interpretation of a series of tests
Let’s suppose you measure a bunch of different RNAs under some experimental condition and get an effect estimate for each one of them. Now, some of them will be over the line and some will be under it and some of the ones under the line are actually relevant effects, whose size may actually be quite similar to those over the line. Naturally, people focus in their interpretation in those effects that they label as “discoveries”, and ignore the rest. And that means that they blithely ignore co-occurrence patterns, for example between genes in the same regulon, that are actually present in their data and can actually be seen in their analysis! Such missed opportunities are solely caused by a bad choice of the analytic method.








Figure G.6: A whole regulon, half of it thrown away. We simulate an experiment measuring ~2500 genes, of which 14 belong to a single regulon and are genuinely co-regulated (all truly up-regulated). Panel A is the usual volcano plot: log2 fold change against -log10(p), with the dashed p = 0.05 line. Genes scatter because each has its own measurement precision. Of the 14 regulon genes, 7 happen to cross the line (filled red, ‘discovered’) and 7 fall just below it (hollow orange) – and in standard practice everything below the line is ignored as a ‘non-discovery’. The split is essentially luck: the lost genes are not different in kind, they were just measured a little less precisely. Panel B reads the regulon as a unit instead of one gene at a time. Every one of the 14 genes is shifted to the right of the genome-wide null (grey density centred on zero) – the whole set moved together. Combining their evidence (Stouffer’s method) gives a set-level p around 2e-11, overwhelmingly more convincing than any single gene’s p value and far beyond the 7 that reached individual significance. The coordinated shift of the regulon is real evidence that sits in the data the whole time; dichotomising gene-by-gene at p = 0.05 simply discards it. This is why pathway- and gene-set-level analyses can see structure that gene-by-gene significance testing misses.







G.8.3 The problem of overblown effects
This is the most troubling of the three, because it leads to the negation of the very principle that gave birth to null hypothesis testing. The idea behind H0 testing is that when a researcher sees an effect, they naturally want to believe in the reality of this effect and may ignore the more likely explanation of sampling error. Thus, running a test and looking at a non-significant p value will cool their head, curb their enthusiasm, and lead to a more honest science in the long run. And this is exactly what should happen, as long as the power of the test to find true effects is high. The power of 0.9, for instance, simply means that out of every 100 true effects (a.k.a. false H0-s), 90 effects on average will come out as “statistically significant”. When the power is >0.9 (>90%), then the magnitude of those sample-based discoveries will on average be very nearly the same as that of the underlying true population effects (a small upward bias remains even at high power, as the simulation below shows). Unfortunately, the true power of the experiment is quite hard to ascertain and a typical power of a biological experiment (especially in animals) tends to be very much lower than 0.9, often residing in the 0.1-0.3 region.12 This leads to overestimated effect sizes of the statistically significant discoveries, because many true effects with correct effect sizes in the sample data will fail to achieve significance; and with a truly low power the ONLY realistic way to achieve statistical significance is to present an overblown effect size and/or deceivingly low variation (the simulation below).
As making discoveries by statistical significance is a long-term commitment, we must admit as a logical fact that the published effect sizes of animal and human studies at least tend to be seriously over-estimated, solely due to the analytic method that was supposed to curb our enthusiasm about the very same effects. The only realistic solution to this that does not entail using more sensible methods is to dramatically increase the sample sizes of what are already some of the most expensive experiments in biomedicine.








Figure G.7: Low power inflates the effects you are allowed to publish (the ‘winner’s curse’). A single true effect (a 5 mm BP reduction, dashed red line) is studied by experiments of differing statistical power; lower power simply means a noisier study (larger standard error). For each power we simulate many studies and then keep only those that reach statistical significance – the ones that would actually be reported as discoveries. Panel A shows the distribution of those significant effect estimates. At full power the significant effects are centred on the true 5 mm. But as power drops, the distribution slides to the right: with low power, the only way for a study to clear the significance threshold is to have drawn, by chance, a large over-estimate (and/or a deceptively small standard error), so every published ‘discovery’ is exaggerated. Panel B summarises this as the average fold-overestimation (the Type M, or magnitude, error): about 1.1x at 90% power but roughly 3.6x at 10% power. Because typical power in much of biomedicine sits in the 0.1-0.3 range, the published effect sizes of significant findings are, on average, systematically too big – exactly the mechanism that makes a single significant study like Drug 3 in the earlier figure (ES = 20 mm) untrustworthy. The procedure meant to curb our enthusiasm instead guarantees inflated effects whenever power is low.







G.8.4 The problem of significance chasing
Suppose a court of law is hearing the evidence and the judge decides to send the case back to gather more of the stuff, because the weight of evidence presented is insufficient to convict. After gathering more evidence, a verdict is reached. If we assume that exculpatory evidence is not buried and all evidence is weighted impartially, then most people would agree, that everything is fine in this simple story. How about when we gather N observations and calculate a p value that lies on the wrong side of significance? It should then be equally all right to collect more data (N+1, N+2, and so on) and recalculate the p value, until significance is reached. Or is it? As it happens, if you do this long enough, then you are virtually certain to get a significant p value sooner or later, even if you are testing a true null. This sad fact means that generations of scientists have been taught that collecting more evidence is a sin. Moreover, those that commit it and chase significance until they find it, will not only have committed a fraud-like infraction, but can also publish their finding as a real thing and get away with it, as it is very hard to prove that someone has calculated many p values and deleted all but one. The apparent paradox around collecting evidence dissolves as soon as we understand that a p value is not a measure of evidence. It measures the concordance of sample data and simulated data under true null, nothing more.








Figure G.8: The dance of the p values, and why chasing significance works. Here there is no effect at all: every data point is drawn from the same null distribution. Panel A follows 12 such studies as they collect subjects one at a time, recomputing the p value after each new subject. The p value does not settle down – it dances all over the range between 0 and 1, wandering below the 0.05 line and back up again purely by chance. A researcher who keeps collecting data and stops the moment the p value dips below 0.05 (black dots) will declare a ‘significant’ discovery even though nothing is there. Panel B runs 1000 such true-null studies and tracks the fraction that have crossed 0.05 at least once by a given sample size. A single, honest test has a 5% false-positive rate (dotted line); but peeking after every subject and stopping at the first ‘significant’ result pushes the false-positive rate to about 35% by n = 150, and it keeps climbing – collect long enough and significance becomes essentially guaranteed. The resolution of the apparent paradox (why is gathering more evidence a sin?) is that a p value is not a measure of accumulating evidence; it measures the agreement between one fixed dataset and the null, so recomputing it as the data grow and stopping on a whim breaks the very long-run guarantee that gives ‘significance’ its meaning.





None of this makes collecting more data a sin in itself – it makes unplanned, peek-until-significant collection a sin. The legitimate way to watch your data accumulate is to plan for it in advance. Group-sequential designs spread the error budget across a set of pre-specified interim analyses (the O’Brien-Fleming and Pocock boundaries are the classic recipes), and alpha-spending functions generalise this to flexible monitoring; either way the overall type I error stays at the nominal level no matter how many planned looks you take, and stopping early for success or futility becomes good practice rather than cheating. It is standard in well-run clinical trials. In the estimation framework the tension largely dissolves: a posterior is simply updated as data arrive, and – provided the decision of when to stop does not itself depend on unmodelled features of the data – the posterior at any moment remains a valid summary of the evidence so far. The sin was never looking at the data; it was looking without accounting for the looking.

title: Appendix G — Null hypothesis testing
section: G.9 The problem of multiple testing
text:
G.9 The problem of multiple testing
If you do over some time or experimental system or field of study k independent tests of k independent samples, and call all tests, whose p<0.05 “significant”, then \(p_{corrected} = p \cdot k\). This is the Bonferroni correction, which fixes the family-wise type I error rate at the level \(\alpha\) (here 0.05). Presenting any results whose \(p \cdot k < 0.05\) (equivalently \(p < 0.05/k\)) as “significant” has the same meaning as presenting a p value from a single test, whose p < 0.05 as “significant”. Thus we fix the family-wise type I error rate at the level \(\alpha\). Alas, this correction leads to a loss of sensitivity (it increases the frequency of type II errors). To mitigate this problem, a host of compromise procedures, like sequential Bonferroni, has been developed. These corrections result in a higher corrected p value, which no longer fixes the type I error level at 0.05, but lead to a smaller drop in sensitivity. Arguably the most serious aspect of the multiple testing problem is that there is no consensus about what constitutes a family of tests. It could be multiple tests done within a single experiment (like measuring the level of 20 000 mRNAs from a sample of 3 biological samples), or all experiment done by you over your lifetime, or all experiments done by various groups within the confines of a single well-defined experimental system, or whatever. Perhaps the best recommendation that can be given is to record and publish all calculated p values. But even this is far from enough, as it has been successfully argued that not only the tests that were done, but also those that would have been done, had data been different, count in the family k.
Multiple testing problem presents a strong reason for abandoning the very concept of “statistical significance” as unworkable in scientific practice. The alternative approach entails Bayesian estimation of sample means and effect sizes, accompanied by measures of estimation uncertainty, which are often presented in the form of 95% credible intervals. Within this approach false alarms are dealt by the prior structures and by using multilevel modelling (Chapter 28).13

G.9.1 Multiple testing without multiple tests: welcome to the Garden of Forking Paths
To conclude, we introduce the garden of forking paths, which is a simile to illustrate that a multiple comparisons problem can persist, even where people perform only a single analysis on a single comparison.14 There can be a large number of potential comparisons when the analyst chooses analytic methods based on the data they see. This means that had the data been different, they would have used a different approach to its analysis, and as the data were what they were, there is no way of knowing how many different analyses were open to the researcher (which depends, obviously, on the size of their analytic repertoire). This presents a kind of multiple testing problem without multiple testing.


G.9.2 From the garden of forking paths to multiverse analysis
One response turns the garden from a problem into a report. A multiverse analysis runs the same comparison under every reasonable combination of data-processing and modelling choices and publishes the whole distribution of results.15 As its authors intended it, this is a transparency device, not a test: it shows how much the conclusion depends on arbitrary choices and which choices matter, and it has proved good at exposing fragility – in one systematic exercise, 8 192 Cox models for each of 417 exposures in a national survey reversed the direction of the association between the 1st and 99th percentile of specifications for 31% of the variables.16 Turning the distribution into a verdict needs a decision rule, and the rule matters: demanding that most specifications be individually significant is vote-counting, whose power falls as noisy specifications are added, whereas a joint test that asks whether the whole specification curve is more extreme than chance borrows strength across specifications and keeps reasonable power.17 Two cautions stand. The specifications share one dataset and are not independent, so agreement among them shows insensitivity to analytic choices, not replicability; and specifications are not exchangeable – some are simply worse, a dichotomised predictor or a dropped confounder – so the degrees of freedom move from “which analysis do I report” to “which analyses do I admit”.18 The book’s own position on fitting several models to one question, and why the choice among them must never be made on the estimate, is set out in Chapter 23 (the section “Several models, one causal question”), where the specification curve appears as the transparent way to report defensible disagreement.


G.9.3 Controlling the false discovery rate
Bonferroni and its relatives control the chance of even one false positive, which is sensible for a handful of tests and ruinous for twenty thousand genes: it throws away nearly every real effect to protect against any false one. The false discovery rate (FDR) of Benjamini and Hochberg controls instead the expected proportion of false positives among the discoveries. Order the \(m\) p values \(p_{(1)} \le p_{(2)} \le \dots \le p_{(m)}\), find the largest \(k\) with \(p_{(k)} \le \tfrac{k}{m}\alpha\), and call the first \(k\) significant; the expected fraction of false discoveries among them is then at most \(\alpha\).19 Storey’s q value refines this by estimating the fraction of true nulls from the flat right-hand part of the p value histogram and reporting, for each feature, the FDR of the list that would just include it. Controlling the FDR still says nothing about whether any particular hypothesis is true – it bounds an average over the list – and the question of what counts as the family remains open.

title: Appendix G — Null hypothesis testing
section: G.10 Connecting the p value to the rest of statistics
text:
G.10 Connecting the p value to the rest of statistics
The p value is wired into the rest of statistics at three points. It carries the same information as a confidence interval, read off at a single spot. It contains the same machinery as regression and the generalised linear model. And, under one very specific assumption, it is a probability statement straight out of Bayes’ theorem. Seeing these wires does two useful things. It demystifies the p value – once you know what it is connected to, its odd behaviour stops being mysterious. And it shows why the estimation-based, Bayesian approach that the rest of this book is built on does not so much reject the p value as contain it: almost every legitimate thing a p value tells you can be recovered from a posterior, usually carrying the interpretation you wanted in the first place.

G.10.1 Connecting the p value to confidence intervals
If your p value is 0.05, a frequentist 95% CI just touches zero. If the p value is 0.1, a 90% CI touches zero; if it is 0.25, a 75% CI touches zero. This is not a coincidence but an identity: the confidence interval and the p value are the same calculation run in two directions.
The p value fixes the null at zero and asks how compatible the data are with it. The confidence interval turns the question around: it slides the null across every possible value and keeps all the null values that the data would not reject. Formally, the X% confidence interval is exactly the set of hypothesised values \(\theta_0\) for which a test of \(H_0:\text{effect}=\theta_0\) gives \(p > 1-X\). Zero is inside the 95% CI precisely when the test of \(H_0:\text{effect}=0\) is non-significant at 0.05 – which is just another way of saying \(p>0.05\). (Note that this is the reverse of a common misstatement: the interval is built by moving the null across the axis, not by centring a null on the sample mean.)
Formally, a 95% confidence interval is a procedure: applied to many samples, 95% of the intervals it produces contain the true value. This is a statement about the long-run performance of the algorithm, not about the interval in hand.20 Under a flat prior and a normal likelihood the 95% confidence interval and the 95% Bayesian credible interval coincide numerically – the same identity that the Type S section below exploits – so a confidence interval can be read as the credible interval of someone who claimed to know nothing beforehand; with any informative prior the two part company, and only the credible interval says what students expect an interval to say (Chapter 10).
So the two carry the same information at the one point they share, the null of zero. But the interval carries that information at every value at once, and that is strictly more useful. The p value collapses the whole picture to a single tail probability at zero; the interval shows the entire range of effect sizes the data are compatible with. This is exactly why Figure G.4 could tell three different stories from one identical p value: the p was silent about size and precision, but the intervals were not. It also pays to drop the word confidence, which invites the misreading that the interval has a 95% chance of containing the true effect (it does not; Chapter 8 gives the coverage reading). A cleaner reading is a compatibility interval: the range of effect sizes reasonably compatible with the data, given the model.21 The curve in Figure G.9 makes this literal – it is a p-value function that reports, for every candidate effect, how compatible it is with the data; cutting it at any height gives the corresponding interval.








Figure G.9: A confidence interval is a p value run backwards. The curve is the p-value function: for every hypothesised effect size on the horizontal axis it gives the p value you would get from testing that value as the null. It peaks at p = 1 over the point estimate (6 mm) – the data are perfectly compatible with the truth being exactly the estimate – and falls away on both sides. Cutting the curve at a height of alpha and reading off the span underneath gives the (1 - alpha) confidence interval: the 0.05 cut spans the 95% CI [2.1, 9.9], the 0.10 cut the narrower 90% CI, the 0.25 cut the narrower-still 75% CI. The interval is thus nothing more than the set of null values the data would not reject. The single ordinary p value – testing the null of zero effect – is just the height of this whole curve at one point (here p = 0.003, red). The p value throws away the rest of the curve; the interval keeps it, which is why the interval, and not the lone p value, tells you about the size and precision of the effect.







G.10.2 Connecting the p value to the t-test, regression and the GLM
Students often learn the t-test, ANOVA, correlation and regression as separate techniques, each with its own p value. They are one technique. A two-group comparison is identical to a linear regression with a single 0/1 predictor coding the group:
\[\text{effect}_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1\,\text{group}_i + \varepsilon_i .\]
Here \(\beta_1\) is the difference in group means, its standard error is the t-test’s standard error, and the p value printed next to it is the t-test’s p value, to the last decimal. One-way ANOVA is the same model with a categorical predictor with 2+ levels; Pearson correlation is the same model on standardised variables; the generalised linear model extends it to non-normal outcomes (Chapter 25). “The p value of a t-test” and “the p value of a regression coefficient” are not an analogy – they are the same number.
What does the Bayesian version look like? Take the same model, but instead of one best-fitting line and a tail probability, put a prior on the coefficients and report the whole posterior of \(\beta_1\). With a flat prior and the normal likelihood, the posterior of the effect is essentially a t-distribution centred on the estimate with the same standard error – so the frequentist interval and the Bayesian posterior land on top of each other (Figure G.10, panel A). The arithmetic is shared; only the interpretation differs, and the Bayesian one is the one you wanted: a distribution of credible effect sizes, from which \(P(\text{effect}>0)\), or \(P(\text{effect}>5\text{ mm})\), can be read off directly.
The payoff of doing it the Bayesian way is that you are no longer locked into the normal error model. Kruschke’s “Bayesian estimation supersedes the t test” (BEST) swaps the normal likelihood for a Student-t likelihood and estimates the mean and the spread (\(\mu\) and \(\sigma\)) jointly, letting the data’s own scatter – including its fat tails – decide how much an extreme point should count.22 The effect is dramatic. In panel B of Figure G.10 we add a single aberrant patient to the same trial. The ordinary t-test (= the Gaussian regression) is dragged from a near-significant p = 0.07 to a thoroughly null p = 0.31, its estimate almost halved by one data point. The robust Student-t model shrugs: its posterior stays put at about 5.9 mm, almost exactly where it sat before the outlier arrived. The robust likelihood is not a trick; it is an honest statement that real measurements occasionally misbehave, and a model that expects this is not held hostage by one of them.








Figure G.10: The t-test is a regression, and its Bayesian upgrade is robust. A one-sample (paired) trial of 15 patients; the effect is the BP reduction on drug versus placebo (positive = good). Panel A: the frequentist 95% confidence interval from the t-test (red, identical to an intercept-only linear regression) and the Bayesian posterior for the mean effect under a flat prior with a normal likelihood (blue) sit on top of each other – same arithmetic, different words. The posterior mean is 5.1 mm and the interval just includes zero (one-sided p = 0.034; posterior P(effect < 0) = 0.039 – nearly the same number, a point we return to next). Panel B: we now add a single aberrant patient (a 25 mm rise in BP). The normal-likelihood model – i.e. the ordinary t-test – is dragged from 5.1 down to about 3.3 mm and from a near-significant p = 0.07 to a firmly null p = 0.31: one patient flips the conclusion. The robust BEST model, which replaces the normal likelihood with a Student-t likelihood and estimates the mean and spread together, stays at about 5.9 mm – essentially unmoved. Same data, same flat prior; the only change is a likelihood that expects the occasional wild point.







G.10.3 Connecting the p value to Bayesian statistics
Earlier in this chapter we insisted that a p value is not the probability that there is no effect, nor the probability that any hypothesis is true. That is correct. But there is one specific construction under which a p value does turn into an honest probability about the parameter – and seeing exactly what that construction requires is the most illuminating connection of all.
Take a one-sided p value: you observed a positive effect and you ask how often the null would produce something this positive or more. Now put a flat prior on the effect (every value equally likely beforehand) and run Bayes’ theorem with the usual normal likelihood. The posterior is a normal distribution centred on your estimate. And the posterior probability that the true effect is actually negative – that you have the sign wrong – comes out exactly equal to the one-sided p value. In Figure G.11, the same 2 mm estimate with SEM 1 mm from Figure G.1 has a one-sided p of 0.023; under a flat prior, the posterior probability that the drug truly raises blood pressure is the same number.
That number is Gelman and Carlin’s Type S (sign) error probability: the probability that a result points the wrong way.23 It is the natural partner of the Type M (magnitude) error we met in Figure G.7 – Type M asks how exaggerated a significant effect is, Type S asks how often it points the wrong way – and together they are the estimation-minded replacement for the old type I / type II bookkeeping.
The crucial word in all this is flat. The clean identity “one-sided p value = posterior probability of the wrong sign” holds only when the prior is flat. A flat prior says you genuinely knew nothing beforehand – not the magnitude, not even the sign. That is almost never true; recall the three-drug example, where a literature of 354 trials told us a great deal about plausible effects. With any realistic prior the two numbers part ways, the posterior usually being more sceptical than the p value. So the reinterpretation does not rescue the p value – it exposes the hidden assumption underneath it. A p value behaves like a Bayesian sign-error probability computed by someone who swore they knew nothing, which is precisely the assumption the rest of this book tries to avoid.








Figure G.11: A one-sided p value is a Type S error probability wearing a flat prior. Both panels use the chapter’s opening result: an observed effect of 2 mm with a standard error of 1 mm. Panel A is the frequentist picture – the H0 sampling distribution centred on zero, with the tail beyond the observed 2 mm shaded; that tail is the one-sided p value, 0.023. Panel B is the Bayesian picture under a flat prior – the posterior is centred on the estimate (2 mm), and the shaded mass to the left of zero is the posterior probability that the true effect is actually negative, i.e. that the drug raises blood pressure. The two shaded areas are mirror images and numerically identical (0.023): the one-sided p value is the flat-prior posterior probability of getting the sign wrong – Gelman and Carlin’s Type S error. The identity holds only for a flat prior; with any realistic prior the two diverge, which is precisely why the choice of prior matters.







G.10.4 Connecting the p value to the weight of evidence
A small p value feels like strong evidence against the null. How much evidence is it really? To answer that we have to compare the null against an alternative – which a p value, computed from the null alone, never does. When the comparison is forced, the verdict is sobering: p values systematically overstate the evidence against the null.
The cleanest way to see this is a calibration that holds across a wide class of reasonable alternatives.24 Translate a p value into the most favourable Bayes factor it could possibly justify – the strongest the evidence against the null could be for any sensible alternative. A Bayes factor never weighs the null on its own; it weighs it against a specific alternative, and its value depends on which alternative you name. The most favourable one is the alternative the most consistent with the data – in effect, the hypothesis, chosen with hindsight, that the true effect is exactly the size you happened to estimate (an alternative whose prior is piled up right where the data landed). No alternative you could have named in advance fits the data better than this best-case-after-the-fact one, so the Bayes factor it yields is an upper bound: it is the strongest the evidence against the null could possibly be, and the evidence for any pre-specified alternative is weaker still. A p of 0.05 results in a maximal Bayes factor of about 2.5 to 1 in favour of an effect, and – if the null and the alternative started out equally likely – leaves the null with at least a 29% posterior probability of being true. Not “5% chance the null is true”, as the number is so often misread, but at best 29%. You have to push to p = 0.005 before the null’s posterior probability drops to 7%.
A second, lighter device makes the same point about a single p value. This is the surprisal, or S-value: \(s = -\log_2(p)\). S value measures the number of consecutive “heads” in fair coin tosses that would be exactly as surprising as the p value. A p of 0.05 gives s = 4.3 bits – about as surprising as four or five heads in a row, which nobody would call extraordinary evidence of a loaded coin. A p of 0.005 is 7.6 bits, a p of 0.001 about 10 bits. Recasting the p value as coin tosses cures the temptation to read “p = 0.05” as near-certainty: it is a mild surprise, no more.
Both devices say what the rest of this section has been saying from different angles. The p value is a tail area – not a measure of evidence and not a probability about a hypothesis. The moment you ask the questions scientists actually care about – how big is the effect, how sure am I of its sign, how strong is the evidence, how probable is the hypothesis – you have left the p value behind and re-entered the world of estimation, intervals, priors and posteriors that the rest of this book is about.








Figure G.12: How much evidence is a small p value, really? A p value is computed from the null alone, so by itself it cannot weigh the null against an alternative. When the comparison is forced, p values turn out to overstate the evidence. Panel A shows the smallest posterior probability the null can have, across a wide class of reasonable alternatives and assuming the null and the alternative were equally likely beforehand (the Sellke-Bayarri-Berger calibration). A p of 0.05 leaves the null with at least a 29% chance of being true – nowhere near the 5% it is so often confused with (dotted line: the misreading ‘P(H0) = p’). You must reach p = 0.005 before the null falls below 7%. Panel B restates a single p value as its surprisal, s = -log2(p): the number of heads in a row in fair coin tossing that would be equally surprising. p = 0.05 is only 4.3 bits – four or five heads, a mild surprise – whereas p = 0.001 is about 10 bits. Both calibrations deliver the same warning: a result that merely clears the 0.05 line is weak evidence, not strong, and is certainly not the probability that the hypothesis is true or false.

title: Appendix G — Null hypothesis testing
text:
G.11 Conclusion
None of this means the p value is worthless. Computed honestly, reported in full – every test, not only the winners – and read as exactly what it is (a statement about the compatibility between one dataset and one null, on the assumptions of the model), it is a legitimate, if narrow, summary. The trouble was never the arithmetic. It is that the questions we care about in science – how large, how certain, how credible – are questions about parameters and hypotheses, while the p value answers a question about data. The remedy is not a better threshold or a cleverer correction; it is to model the effect you care about and report its posterior.25

title: Appendix G — Null hypothesis testing
text:
G.12 Key points

The frequentist framework puts the probability on datasets, not hypotheses: a sampling distribution describes what a statistic would do over imagined repetitions, and its spread for a mean is the SEM \(= \sigma/\sqrt{N}\), estimated from the sample – which is why the t distribution replaces the normal at small \(N\).
The central limit theorem is a limit statement, not a rule about \(N\): means of a skewed parent are still skewed at \(N = 30\) (Table G.1).
A p value is the probability, under a point null, of data at least as extreme as those observed. It is not the probability that the null is true, not the probability of any hypothesis, and not a measure of effect size or bias.
Statistical significance is a decision rule with long-run error rates: \(\alpha\) fixes the type I rate, power the sensitivity, and the threshold is a chosen trade-off, not a fact about nature. The fraction of significant results that are false depends on the base rate of true effects among the hypotheses tested.
Same p, different effects: the p value is silent about size and precision; the interval is not. A large p is not evidence of no effect; equivalence testing, or an interval inside the equivalence margin, is.
Dichotomising at a threshold creates the problems: two effects on opposite sides of the line need not differ (Gelman–Stern); a co-regulated set is thrown half away; low power inflates the effects that pass (Type M); and peeking until significance guarantees it, unless the looks are planned.
Multiplicity has no natural family: Bonferroni controls the family-wise rate, the false discovery rate controls the proportion of false discoveries, and the garden of forking paths shows the problem persists with a single reported test.
The p value is wired into the rest of statistics: the confidence interval is the set of nulls not rejected (a p-value function cut at \(\alpha\)); the t-test is a regression; a one-sided p equals the flat-prior posterior probability of the wrong sign (Type S); and the Sellke bound and the S-value show that p = 0.05 is weak evidence.

title: Appendix H — Challenges to the Bayesian position
text:
H.1 A single-event probability “says nothing”
The first objection holds that a probability attached to a one-off event — the result of one election, whether a particular patient survives the year — is empty, because a single event has no long-run frequency. As a claim about meaning, Chapter 8 has answered it: on the belief road \(P(A)\) grades a state of knowledge, and the weather and patient examples of that chapter used such probabilities throughout. Importing the frequency definition and then noting that a single case has no frequency assumes the conclusion.
A real point concerns evaluation, not meaning. A single probabilistic forecast cannot be checked against its single outcome: a forecast of 0.7 for an event that then fails to occur is not thereby shown wrong, because events assigned probability 0.3 occur about thirty per cent of the time. Judging whether a source’s probabilities are any good requires many of them, and a score that rewards calibration — the long-run agreement between stated probabilities and observed frequencies — of which the Brier score is the original example.1 The 2016 United States presidential election, often offered as a failure of probabilistic forecasting, marks the distinction: the better-calibrated forecasts gave the eventual winner, Donald Trump, the higher probability of 0.3, and the public error was to read a probability of 0.7 for the losing candidate, Hilary Clinton, as near-certainty. Stated carefully, the objection is not that single-event probabilities are meaningless but that they cannot be validated one at a time. That is correct — calibration is assessed over a forecaster’s whole record (Chapter 2), where the interval version of the same measurement, and the reasons an interval-production task cannot be scored properly at all, are set out in detail.

title: Appendix H — Challenges to the Bayesian position
section: H.2 Radical uncertainty and the prior
text:
H.2 Radical uncertainty and the prior
A deeper objection holds that in many real settings a prior cannot be set at all, so the calculation never starts. It has a serious lineage: Knight separated risk, where the odds are known, from uncertainty, where they are not2; Keynes held that for some questions “we simply do not know”3; and Kay and King argue that economic and political decisions are typically non-repeatable and non-stationary, so attaching a number to them is false precision rather than information4.
The part of this objection with force is a result, which needs a bit of background. While a hard-to-elicit prior is merely a practical hurdle, the more serious attack claims that there are reasonable preferences which cannot be represented by a prior at all. Understanding its bite requires a result that points the other way: that a rational agent’s choices already contain a prior, stated or not. That result is Savage’s, whose construction does not begin with probabilities, but with an agent’s preferences among acts — options whose payoff depends on which state of the world turns out to hold — together with a small set of axioms those preferences are required to obey. A representation theorem follows: any agent whose preferences obey these axioms behaves as if they had attached a single probability to each state and a utility to each payoff, and then ranked acts by expected utility. The prior is therefore not an input to the theory but a consequence of it. In other words, the existence of a subjective prior is a theorem about coherent preferences, not an ad hoc assumption.
One of those axioms is the sure-thing principle: if two acts yield the same payoff across some set of states, the preference between the acts must not depend on what that shared payoff is — so the states on which the acts agree can be set aside, and the choice made on the states where they differ.5 Ellsberg built a wager on which reasonable people violate it.6
An urn holds 90 balls: 30 are red, and the other 60 are black or yellow in a proportion no one is told. The states are the colour drawn; an act is a bet that pays £100 on the colours it names and £0 otherwise. Consider four such bets (Table H.1):

Only the share of red is known (30/90), so the bets on red and on black or yellow carry known odds, while the bets on black and on red or yellow carry unknown ones. Offered the choice, most people take the bet on red over the bet on black, and the bet on black or yellow over the bet on red or yellow — the known odds each time.
The two ideas now bite. By the representation theorem, anyone holding a single prior for the urn — treating the 60 unknown balls as, say, 30 black and 30 yellow — would score each bet by its chance of paying and rank the four once and for all. By the sure-thing principle, the first two bets agree on yellow (both pay 0), and the last two are those same two bets with the yellow payoff raised to 100 for both; yellow is a shared payoff within each pair, so it should cancel, and the red-versus-black ranking should carry over to the (red-or-yellow)-versus-(black-or-yellow) ranking. The observed choices reverse it. Equivalently, preferring the bet on red requires \(P(\text{red}) > P(\text{black})\), while preferring the bet on black-or-yellow requires \(P(\text{black}) > P(\text{red})\); no prior satisfies both. The preferences are stable and widely shared, yet no single prior represents them — the gap the objection points to. This ambiguity aversion is reproducible and arguably rational, so it places such preferences outside the scope of Savage’s theorem: “I cannot fix a sharp prior” is then a position the axioms do not exclude, not a confusion about probability.
The orthodox reply is to add a level. If the composition of the urn is unknown, put a prior over it — and in this symmetric problem any prior that treats black and yellow alike forces the predictive probabilities to \(P(\text{red}) = P(\text{black}) = P(\text{yellow}) = 1/3\), whereupon the ambiguity disappears and the problem reduces to ordinary risk. This is de Finetti’s reduction: beliefs about an unknown frequency, weighted by a prior over its values, collapse to a single predictive distribution. The move is available, and here the choice of second-order prior does not even matter, because symmetry fixes the answer. Two things limit it. First, the reduced model predicts indifference between the urns, which is not what people do; it recommends against the phenomenon rather than accounting for it. Second, the symmetry is special — in an asymmetric problem the predictive probabilities depend on the parametrisation of the “ignorance” prior, the difficulty Chapter 8 noted for objective priors. Whether ambiguity may always be reduced to risk in this way is the contested step, and the models below take the other branch.

title: Appendix H — Challenges to the Bayesian position
section: H.3 Sets of priors: imprecise probability and robust Bayes
text:
H.3 Sets of priors: imprecise probability and robust Bayes
If a single sharp prior overstates what is known, the response that keeps the calculus is to carry a set of priors rather than one. A closed set of distributions — a credal set — assigns each event a lower and an upper probability, \(\underline P(A) = \inf_p p(A)\) and \(\overline P(A) = \sup_p p(A)\) over the set; the width \(\overline P(A) - \underline P(A)\) records how little is known, and is zero only when the set collapses to a point and probability becomes precise. Total ignorance is the vacuous set, \(\underline P(A) = 0\) and \(\overline P(A) = 1\) — which is what ignorance looks like, in contrast to the uniform prior, a definite symmetric commitment that Chapter 8 warned against confusing with it.
Two traditions develop this with the same mathematics and different emphasis. Imprecise probability rebuilds the foundations: where de Finetti’s agent posts one fair price for a gamble, Walley’s agent posts two — a highest buying price and a lowest selling price — and declines to trade in between, so the betting argument of Chapter 8 generalises by dropping the assumption that every gamble has a single fair price.7 A concrete instance is the imprecise Dirichlet model for proportions, which begins vacuous and contracts as data accumulate.8 Robust Bayes keeps ordinary Bayes but, conceding that one prior cannot be pinned down, specifies a class of priors, recomputes the posterior quantity for each, and reports the range; a narrow range means the conclusion is insensitive to the prior, a wide one that the data do not determine it.9 This is the global form of the sensitivity analysis Chapter 8 endorsed. A decision still has to be made from a set, and one rule is maxmin expected utility: score each option by its expected utility under the least favourable prior in the set — its worst case over the priors entertained — and choose the option whose worst case is best.10 In Ellsberg’s urn this reproduces the preference for known odds, because a bet on a known colour has a value every prior agrees on, whereas a bet on an unknown colour is judged by the composition least favourable to it. A separate limit is worth keeping in view: every guarantee here holds relative to the set of models entertained, and if the data-generating process lies outside all of them, coherence no longer ensures the conclusion is correct.11

title: Appendix H — Challenges to the Bayesian position
text:
H.4 Dilation
Carrying a set of priors has a consequence with no analogue in single-prior analysis, and it bears directly on later chapters. Ordinarily, data narrow beliefs. With a set of priors, conditioning on an observation can widen the interval: for some partitions one can know in advance that, whichever cell is observed, the posterior interval for a proposition will be wider than the prior interval. This is dilation.12
A fair coin is to be tossed, so the probability of heads is \(1/2\). A second person announces a prediction of the toss, but nothing is known of their reliability — the credal set admits everything from a perfect predictor to a perfect anti-predictor. Before the prediction is revealed the probability of heads is \(1/2\); after it is revealed, the conditional probability of heads ranges over the whole interval from near 0 to near 1, because the set contains distributions under which the prediction is highly informative in either direction. An uninterpretable signal from a source of unknown reliability widens a probability that was previously sharp, and one could have foreseen that any prediction would do so.
Dilation is not an inconsistency: the model stays coherent, and no sure loss can be made against it. Whether it is a defect or a virtue is disputed. Read as a defect, an inference that becomes less certain on data looks pathological. Read as a virtue, the precise \(1/2\) was the artefact — it relied on an unstated assumption that the prediction was independent of the coin, and once that assumption is withdrawn the wide interval is the faithful report. The phenomenon also corrects a natural assumption about robust Bayes: because robust Bayes updates a set of priors by the same rule, it dilates too. Where a robust-Bayes analysis shows no dilation, it is because the class was anchored tightly to an informative base prior — that is, more was assumed than the radical-uncertainty objection grants. One cannot claim both deep ignorance, which requires a wide set, and immunity from dilation, which requires a narrow one.
The phenomenon has a direct counterpart in applied work. When the sign or magnitude of a bias — unmeasured confounding, an unknown selection mechanism — is genuinely not known, an analysis that represents that ignorance faithfully can yield bounds the data fail to narrow, and that may widen on further conditioning. This is the logic of partial identification and of the sensitivity analyses developed in Chapter 20; dilation is the same fact stated at the level of belief.

title: Appendix H — Challenges to the Bayesian position
text:
H.5 Is ambiguity aversion irrational?
The biases catalogued in Chapter 2 — base-rate neglect, the conjunction fallacy, anchoring — are departures from probability or expected-utility theory that people renounce once the structure is pointed out. It is tempting to file ambiguity aversion alongside them, as one more failure to reason coherently. There is a strong argument for doing so, due to Raiffa: if you are indifferent between betting on red and betting on black in the unknown urn, decide the colour by a fair coin; the resulting mixture has a known one-half chance of paying, matching the known urn, so a coherent agent should not prefer one urn to the other.13 On this view ambiguity aversion forgoes a sure equivalence, and it does attenuate with incentives and learning.
Two features distinguish it from the Chapter 2 biases. It survives reflection: sophisticated agents shown the argument frequently continue to prefer known odds and defend the preference, whereas the mark of a fallacy is that one abandons it once it is seen. And it has been given normative, not merely descriptive, axiomatisations — Choquet expected utility14, maxmin expected utility15, and smooth-ambiguity preferences16 are theories of rational choice that weaken the sure-thing principle deliberately, and it has been argued that committing to a precise prior one has no information to justify is itself the less rational course.17 Whether ambiguity aversion is irrational therefore turns on whether Savage’s axioms are taken as constitutive of rationality or as one model of it — and this book has already taken the modest view, that probability theory captures an important part of rational thinking rather than the whole of it. On that view the cleaner classification is not that ambiguity aversion fails to meet the standard, but that it disputes which standard applies.

title: Appendix H — Challenges to the Bayesian position
text:
H.6 The position taken here
None of these challenges refutes the calculus; each bounds the scope of one way of using it. Single-event probabilities are meaningful and are validated over many forecasts, not one. Under radical uncertainty a sharp prior may not be available, and a set of priors with a stated decision rule is the disciplined response, at the price of phenomena such as dilation. Ambiguity aversion is better read as a rival standard than as a mistake. For the work in this book — finite data, models with declared structure, priors that must survive criticism and sensitivity analysis — a single prior, varied and checked, is adequate, and is what the later chapters use; the apparatus of sets of priors is held in reserve for the cases, flagged where they arise, in which a single prior would assert more than is known. The aim is unchanged from the first page of Chapter 8: to quantify the uncertainty that can be quantified, and to mark plainly the uncertainty that cannot.

title: Appendix H — Challenges to the Bayesian position
text:
H.7 Exercises

The second-order prior in Ellsberg’s urn. Take the 90-ball urn (30 red; 60 black or yellow, unknown split). Put a prior on the number of black balls that is symmetric in black and yellow, and show that the predictive probabilities are \(P(\text{red}) = P(\text{black}) = P(\text{yellow}) = 1/3\), so an expected-utility agent is indifferent within each pair of bets in the table. State which empirical fact this prediction fails to match, and name a decision rule that reproduces the observed preference for known odds.
Dilation. In the coin-and-predictor example, explain why learning the prediction widens the interval for “heads” from the point \(1/2\) to almost all of \([0, 1]\), and identify the single assumption a precise-prior analysis would have to add to keep the probability at \(1/2\). Does robust Bayes avoid the widening, and why?

text:
